## Available Tools

The six analysis capabilities are shared across both transports, but the exposed MCP names are intentionally transport-specific: hosted/Worker connections use the `visibility.*` namespace, while the local stdio package uses flat names.

| Hosted / Worker | Local stdio | What it does | What you provide |
|---|---|---|---|
| `visibility.check` | `check_visibility` | Latest stored AI visibility snapshot for selected engines and optionally one request-mode cohort, with per-engine scores, winning prompts, and losing prompts. | `brand_id`, optional `engines[]`, `measurement_mode` (`model_only` or `search_requested`), `run_mode` (`live` or `batch`), `active_prompts_only` |
| `visibility.history` | `get_visibility_history` | Daily/weekly stored visibility trends with prompt-roster and model-only/search-requested evidence. Optional `current_identity_only=true` excludes old-identity/unattributable runs, and `active_prompts_only=true` scores only currently active buyer questions. Retired-only runs are unmeasured; historical defaults stay unchanged. Scope metadata discloses exclusions and measurement limitations. | `brand_id`, optional `days` (default 30), `granularity` (`daily`/`weekly`), `current_identity_only` and `active_prompts_only` (both default `false`) |
| `visibility.compare` | `compare_competitors` | Recorded share-of-voice with brand-only, co-mentioned and competitor-only evidence. `observation_coverage.per_engine` discloses successful responses, distinct runs/prompts and latest observation time for each observed engine so uneven sampling is visible; absent engines are not measured zeros. `identity_attribution` excludes old-identity run evidence from current comparison shares using the run start time (even when a response was captured later), while preserving historical runs. `outside_current_tracking` and `historical_coverage_note` warn when historical competitor coverage cannot be verified (new domains are not retroactively scored). | `brand_id`, optional `competitor_domains[]`, optional `days` |
| `visibility.citations` | `get_citations` | Paginated citation events — prompt, engine, excerpt, citation type and brand URL when present. Optional selected `engines`, current-identity and active buyer-prompt cohorts filter citation pages and source rankings before pagination; historical all-engine default retained. | `brand_id`, optional `days`, legacy single `engine` or `engines` (not both), `limit` (1-100), `current_identity_only` and `active_prompts_only` (both default `false`), `cursor` |
| `visibility.content_gaps` | `get_content_gaps` | Evidence-grounded recommendations with `losing_prompt_evidence` listing bounded stored prompt/run/response identifiers for auditing observed competitor-only losses (record references, **not verified citations**). `observation_coverage` reports usable active-prompt counts, each engine's run as-of time (`refreshed_at`; completion or start if unfinished), and `unmeasured_engines` with no usable selected-cohort/current-identity responses (including all-error runs and scans excluded after a name/domain/alias/exclusion change). `identity_attribution.stale_engines` identifies excluded pre-change scans; historical runs remain available. Neither an as-of timestamp nor an absent engine proves a successful full scan. Optional `measurement_mode` chooses each engine's latest eligible model-only or search-requested stored run, with the selection disclosed in `measurement_scope.measurement_mode_filter`; omission retains legacy mixed evidence. Neither mode proves a citation. `configuration_comparability` warns when usable scans predate brand-settings updates (possibly refresh cadence only). Optional Claude Haiku analysis requires explicit opt-in. | `brand_id`, optional `engines`, `measurement_mode` (`model_only` or `search_requested`), `max_recommendations` (1-10), `ai_analysis` (default `false`; `true` incurs Anthropic token charges and may retry once) |
| `visibility.refresh` | `refresh_brand` | Manually trigger a fresh scan across every engine whose API key is set. | `brand_id`, optional `engines[]` filter |

Citation pages default to 50 rows; when `has_more=true`, send the returned `next_cursor` with the same `brand_id`, `days`, `engine` or `engines`, `current_identity_only` and `active_prompts_only` selections. A current-identity cursor becomes invalid if the tracked identity boundary changes, an active-prompt cursor if the active prompt IDs change, and an engine-scoped cursor if its selected engine set changes; restart from page one. Previously issued historical cursors remain supported. Pagination uses observation timestamps and stable run/prompt/response identifiers, not shifting offsets, and holds the first page's time window fixed. `top_sources` summarizes the entire selected window/cohort, not only the current page. `measurement_modes` distinguishes model-only from search-requested observations; neither mode proves the URL was independently verified. No extra provider requests are made to page stored evidence.

Competitor comparisons retain the legacy `prompts_you_win` field for compatibility; it means **any brand mention**, including responses also mentioning competitors. Use `prompts_brand_only` for brand mentions without tracked competitors and `prompts_co_mentioned` for brand-plus-competitor responses. The cohorts are classified per engine response, so the same prompt can appear in both across different engines. Competitor `prompts_won_against_you` records competitor mentions when the brand is absent; neither field proves an exclusive ranking or recommendation.

The local stdio CLI (npx, desktop extension, Docker) additionally provides brand management — on a Workers deployment the same operations live behind the `X-Seed-Secret`-gated `/admin/*` routes instead:

| Tool (local CLI only) | What it does | What you provide |
|---|---|---|
| `track_brand` | Start tracking a brand with three provider-free category-anchored prompts by default. Returns `starter_prompt_limitations`: an absent category uses brand-name placeholders that may bias visibility scores; even category-specific starters need review. `prompt_generation='anthropic'` explicitly opts in to token-billed Claude generation (at most two attempts). | `brand_id`, `name`, `domain`, optional `category`, `competitors[]`, `aliases[]`, `exclude_terms[]`, `prompt_generation` (`fallback` default or `anthropic`), `prompt_count` (Anthropic only), `refresh_frequency` (`daily`/`weekly`/`manual`, default `weekly`) |
| `update_brand` | Correct an existing brand's domain, name, category, competitors, aliases, exclusions, or refresh cadence without replacing active prompts or historical runs. Set cadence to `manual` to pause scheduled Worker scans while keeping manual refresh available. | `brand_id` plus any fields to change |
| `list_brands` | List tracked brands with domains, competitors, aliases, exclusions, and active prompt counts. | — |
| `list_prompts` | Inspect the exact active buyer-intent prompts for a tracked brand without changing them. | `brand_id` |
| `set_prompts` | Replace the active prompt set with exact user-supplied buyer questions while preserving historical runs. | `brand_id`, `prompts[]` (1-50 unique questions) |
| `generate_prompts` | Regenerate a brand's prompt set via Claude Haiku (replaces active prompts, keeps history). | `brand_id`, optional `count` (default 20) |

## Getting Started

### Step 1 — Get API keys

Engines are opt-in. Pick the ones you want; the rest skip silently.

- **OpenAI** — ChatGPT engine (`gpt-5-search-api`) with web search. OpenAI currently bills web search at $10 per 1,000 calls plus model token charges; see [API pricing](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/pricing) and [API keys](https://platform.openai.com/api-keys).
- **Anthropic** — Claude engine, plus prompt generation and opt-in content-gap analysis (Claude Haiku 4.5). `get_content_gaps` is provider-free unless `ai_analysis=true`; that explicit option can make up to two token-billed API calls. Anthropic prices Haiku 4.5 by input/output tokens; review current [Claude pricing](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/pricing) before estimating scan cost. [console.anthropic.com](https://console.anthropic.com/)
- **Google AI Studio (Gemini)** — Gemini engine (`gemini-3.1-flash-lite`). Google currently offers free-tier token usage for this model, while paid usage is token-priced. Rate limits vary by model, project, and usage tier, and Google says actual capacity can vary; check your project's active limits in AI Studio rather than relying on a fixed RPM/RPD assumption. See [Gemini pricing](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/pricing) and [rate limits](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/rate-limits).
- **Perplexity** — Agent API `fast` preset for grounded web-search visibility. Paid API usage; pricing depends on the preset workload, so check current Agent API pricing before estimating scan cost. [Perplexity Agent API](https://docs.perplexity.ai/docs/agent-api/quickstart) · [pricing](https://docs.perplexity.ai/docs/getting-started/pricing)
- **xAI** — Grok engine (`grok-4.7`) with required Web Search grounding. xAI currently prices Web Search at $5 per 1,000 calls plus model tokens. [console.x.ai](https://console.x.ai/) · [pricing](https://docs.x.ai/developers/pricing)
- **SerpAPI** — Google AI Overviews plus optional Google AI Mode. One SerpAPI key powers both, but AI Mode is deliberately off by default because it adds a separate paid search per prompt; set `SERPAPI_AI_MODE_ENABLED=true` when you want that seventh surface. [Google AI Mode API](https://serpapi.com/google-ai-mode-api) · [serpapi.com/dashboard](https://serpapi.com/dashboard)

Google AI Overviews and AI Mode currently sample **US location and English interface** (`gl=us`, `hl=en`). This does not measure worldwide or multilingual visibility. `check_visibility`, `get_visibility_history`, and `get_citations` return `google_search_sampling` when Google evidence is represented (or a Google citation engine is explicitly requested), so downstream reports can retain this geographic qualification. This metadata does not trigger another provider request.

**Recommended starting pair: OpenAI + Anthropic (Claude).** OpenAI provides grounded ChatGPT visibility through web search and bills search calls plus model tokens; Anthropic also powers prompt generation and content-gap analysis. Review current provider pricing before estimating recurring scan cost. Add Gemini, Perplexity, Grok, or SerpAPI deliberately once you want more coverage; Gemini capacity varies by model, project, and usage tier, and Google AI Overviews often returns no result (scored as a zero). Google AI Mode is a separate SerpAPI call and stays disabled until `SERPAPI_AI_MODE_ENABLED=true`, preventing an existing SerpAPI setup from silently doubling Google search calls.

### Step 2 — Deploy to your Cloudflare account

The deploy is 6 commands and takes about 5 minutes. See [SETUP.md](https://github.com/AKzar1el/mcp-geo/blob/main/SETUP.md) for the full walkthrough with explanations and troubleshooting, or follow the quick version below.

```bash
# 1. Install deps
npm install

# 2. Log in to Cloudflare
npx wrangler login

# 3. Copy the config template
cp wrangler.example.jsonc wrangler.jsonc

# 4. Create KV namespace + D1 database, paste each printed id into wrangler.jsonc
npx wrangler kv namespace create OAUTH_KV
npx wrangler d1 create mcp-geo-db

# 5. Set the required secret + at least one engine API key
#    Recommended starting pair — OpenAI uses web search plus model tokens; check current pricing:
npx wrangler secret put SEED_SECRET
npx wrangler secret put CONNECT_SECRET      # required for hosted OAuth authorization (see SECURITY.md)
npx wrangler secret put OPENAI_API_KEY      # ChatGPT engine
npx wrangler secret put ANTHROPIC_API_KEY   # Claude engine + prompt generation

# 6. Apply migrations and deploy
npx wrangler d1 migrations apply mcp-geo-db --remote
npx wrangler deploy
```

After deploying your own Worker, use that deployment's `/mcp` URL as the
remote endpoint, for example:

```
https://YOUR-WORKER-NAME.YOUR-SUBDOMAIN.workers.dev/mcp
```

Use your configured Worker URL for directory or client integrations. The
public `geo-mcp.digestseo.com/mcp` endpoint is not a no-key hosted substitute
for a deployment with engine provider credentials.

### Step 3 — Connect to your MCP client

After `wrangler deploy` finishes, you get a URL like
`https://digestseo-mcp.YOUR-SUBDOMAIN.workers.dev`.

#### Claude.ai (web)

Settings → Connectors → Add custom connector. Paste:

```
https://YOUR-WORKER-NAME.YOUR-SUBDOMAIN.workers.dev/mcp
```

Complete the OAuth handshake. The connector turns green when ready.

#### ChatGPT (remote MCP)

ChatGPT custom MCP apps connect to remote MCP servers, so use the `/mcp` URL
from your configured Worker deployment above. In ChatGPT, enable Developer
Mode/custom apps for your workspace and add that remote MCP URL. Availability
depends on your ChatGPT plan and workspace admin policy; OpenAI's current MCP
support does not require special `search` or `fetch` tool names.

```
https://YOUR-WORKER-NAME.YOUR-SUBDOMAIN.workers.dev/mcp
```

#### ChatGPT (local/private via OpenAI Secure MCP Tunnel)

OpenAI Secure MCP Tunnel is the supported bridge when you want ChatGPT to use
the local stdio package without exposing it as a public HTTPS server. Create a
tunnel in OpenAI Platform first, then keep `tunnel-client` running on the same
machine that launches mcp-geo. You need a tunnel ID, a tunnel runtime API key,
and ChatGPT developer-mode/tunnel permissions for the target workspace.

Make whichever provider keys you want to use available to the mcp-geo process,
then initialize a tunnel profile with the local package command:

```text
tunnel-client init --sample sample_mcp_stdio_local --profile digestseo --tunnel-id tunnel_0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef --mcp-command "npx -y @digestseo/mcp-geo"
tunnel-client doctor --profile digestseo --explain
tunnel-client run --profile digestseo
```

While `tunnel-client run` is healthy, create a developer-mode app in ChatGPT,
choose **Tunnel** as the connection type, and select that tunnel. This path is
for private/local use; it does not publish mcp-geo as a public ChatGPT app.
Follow OpenAI's current [Secure MCP Tunnel guide](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/secure-mcp-tunnels) for tunnel creation, permissions, downloads, and troubleshooting.

## Environment Variables Reference

| Variable | Required | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `OPENAI_API_KEY` | opt-in | unset | Enables the ChatGPT engine. Without it, ChatGPT is skipped. |
| `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` | opt-in | unset | Enables the Claude engine and permits explicitly requested prompt generation (`prompt_generation='anthropic'`) and content-gap analysis (`ai_analysis=true`). Merely configuring a key does not opt in to these helper calls. |
| `GEMINI_API_KEY` | opt-in | unset | Enables the Gemini engine. Rate limits vary by model, project, and usage tier; check the project's active limits in Google AI Studio (see Troubleshooting). |
| `PERPLEXITY_API_KEY` | opt-in | unset | Enables the Perplexity Agent API `fast` preset. Paid API usage; check current Agent API pricing. |
| `XAI_API_KEY` | opt-in | unset | Enables the Grok engine (`grok-4.7`) with required Web Search grounding. |
| `SERPAPI_API_KEY` | opt-in | unset | Enables Google AI Overviews via SerpAPI. Also provides the credential for Google AI Mode when the explicit flag below is enabled. |
| `SERPAPI_AI_MODE_ENABLED` | no | `false` | Set to `true` to add Google AI Mode as a separate visibility engine. It stays off by default to avoid unexpected extra SerpAPI calls/cost. |
| `SEED_SECRET` | **yes** | unset | Shared secret that gates every `/admin/*` route. Pick a high-entropy string. |
| `CONNECT_SECRET` | **yes (hosted OAuth)** | unset | The OAuth authorization endpoint returns HTTP 503 until this secret is configured. The browser flow then requires it before issuing a token. Existing OAuth tokens are not automatically revoked. See [SECURITY.md](https://github.com/AKzar1el/mcp-geo/blob/main/SECURITY.md). |
| `TURNSTILE_SITE_KEY` | no | unset | Reserved for forks that add a public `/check` form. Unused by the OSS build. |
| `TURNSTILE_SECRET_KEY` | no | unset | Same — reserved for forks. |

Provider credentials are set via `wrangler secret put VAR` in production or `.dev.vars` locally. `SERPAPI_AI_MODE_ENABLED` is a non-secret runtime flag and may be stored under Wrangler `vars` or set in the local process environment.

## Architecture

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    C["MCP client<br/>(Claude.ai / Claude Code / Cursor / ...)"] -- "MCP over HTTP + OAuth" --> W["Cloudflare Worker<br/>digestseo-mcp"]
    CRON["Cron Trigger<br/>every 6h"] --> W
    W --> MCP["Stateless MCP handler<br/>(SDK v2, 6 hosted tools)"]
    W -- "one self-fetch per engine<br/>via SELF service binding" --> RE["/admin/run-engine<br/>(own invocation per engine)"]
    RE --> E1["OpenAI"]
    RE --> E2["Anthropic"]
    RE --> E3["Gemini"]
    RE --> E4["Perplexity"]
    RE --> E5["xAI<br/>(Grok)"]
    RE --> E6["SerpAPI<br/>(AI Overviews / AI Mode)"]
    RE --> DB[("D1<br/>brands / prompts / runs /<br/>responses / cache")]
    MCP --> DB
```

The legacy `GeoMcpAgent` / `MCP_OBJECT` Durable Object binding is retained temporarily for migration compatibility, but current `/mcp` traffic is served by the stateless SDK v2 handler shown above.

Each engine runs in its own Worker invocation with its own free-plan 50-subrequest budget; results are flushed in a single `D1.batch()` per engine. The whole system fits the Cloudflare free tier for a single brand on a daily cadence.

## Security

- `/admin/*` is gated by `SEED_SECRET` (constant-time compared).
- `/mcp` requires OAuth; `CONNECT_SECRET` is required for new authorization grants. Without it, `/authorize` fails closed with HTTP 503. Connected clients can call `visibility.refresh` and spend your engine API credits, so protect and rotate the secret if compromised. Existing OAuth tokens are not revoked automatically.
- Engine keys live in Cloudflare's encrypted secret store, and brands, scan history, and cached responses are stored in your own D1 database. Scan prompts are sent to the AI providers you configure; see the [Privacy Policy](#privacy-policy).

Full details and vulnerability reporting: [SECURITY.md](https://github.com/AKzar1el/mcp-geo/blob/main/SECURITY.md).

## Troubleshooting

- **Worker deploys but tools return empty data** — at least one engine API key is missing. Check `wrangler secret list` and add the keys you intend to use. Engines without keys are silently skipped, which can leave `visibility.check` with no data.
- **`no engines available` error in logs** — no engine API keys are set at all. Set at least one of `OPENAI_API_KEY`, `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, `GEMINI_API_KEY`, `PERPLEXITY_API_KEY`, `XAI_API_KEY`, `SERPAPI_API_KEY`.
- **D1 migration fails** — make sure you've run `npx wrangler d1 migrations apply mcp-geo-db --remote` (and also `--local` for `wrangler dev`). For ad-hoc fixes, `npx wrangler d1 execute mcp-geo-db --remote --file=migrations/0001_initial.sql`.
- **Custom MCP connector in Claude.ai not connecting** — the URL must end in `/mcp`. The hosted OAuth step requires `CONNECT_SECRET`: if `/authorize` returns HTTP 503, configure it with `npx wrangler secret put CONNECT_SECRET`; then enter it in the browser form. If the flow loops, clear the connector and re-add it. Double-check the Worker is publicly reachable (`curl https://YOUR-WORKER-NAME.YOUR-SUBDOMAIN.workers.dev/healthz` should return `ok`).
- **Cron not firing** — check the Cloudflare dashboard at **Workers & Pages → digestseo-mcp → Settings → Triggers**. The "Cron Triggers" section should list `0 */6 * * *`. If it's missing, run `npx wrangler deploy` again — the trigger is registered on deploy. The handler also only dispatches engines for brands whose `refresh_frequency` cadence has elapsed, so a freshly-seeded brand might not fire on the next 6h boundary.
- **`401 unauthorized` from `/admin/*`** — `X-Seed-Secret` header is missing or doesn't match the deployed `SEED_SECRET`. Re-run `npx wrangler secret put SEED_SECRET` and update your `.env.test`.
- **Worker returns 404 on self-fetch / error code 1042** — the `services` binding in `wrangler.jsonc` is missing or the `service` name doesn't match the worker's `name` field. `/admin/run-live` self-fetches `/admin/run-engine` via `env.SELF` (a Cloudflare service binding) precisely because a public-URL fetch back to your own `workers.dev` hostname is blocked by Cloudflare's "Worker called itself" guard. Confirm the `wrangler.jsonc` you deployed contains `"services": [{ "binding": "SELF", "service": "<your-worker-name>" }]` with the same name you set in the top-level `"name"` field. After fixing, `npx wrangler deploy` and re-run.
- **Gemini rate limit (HTTP 429) on prompts** — Gemini API limits vary by model, project, and usage tier, and Google notes that actual capacity can vary. Check the project's current limits in [Google AI Studio](https://aistudio.google.com/) and Google's [rate-limit documentation](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/rate-limits). When a request is rate-limited, mcp-geo records that engine row as failed and excludes it from successful scoring. Google recommends waiting and retrying after a short period or reducing request rate; if the limit is consistently too low for your scan cadence, consider an appropriate paid tier rather than assuming a universal free-tier RPM/RPD quota.
- **`FOREIGN KEY constraint failed` in wrangler tail during `/admin/run-engine`** — the handler defensively `INSERT OR IGNORE`s the runs row before persisting prompt responses. This is an idempotency/FK guard for independently dispatched engine work, so you should not see this on the 0.2.0+ build; if you do, confirm you've deployed the latest `src/index.ts` (`grep -n "INSERT OR IGNORE INTO runs" src/index.ts` should match).

---

## Contributing

Issues and PRs welcome. See [CONTRIBUTING.md](https://github.com/AKzar1el/mcp-geo/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md) for the short version.

---

## Privacy Policy

Full policy for the local package and Claude Desktop extension: https://geo-mcp.digestseo.com/privacy

When you run `digestseo-mcp` locally (npx, the desktop extension, or Docker), all of your data — brands, prompts, runs, responses, and the response cache — stays on your machine in a local SQLite database at `~/.digestseo/digestseo.sqlite` (override with `DIGESTSEO_DB_PATH`). The scan prompts are sent only to the AI providers whose API keys you configure (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Perplexity, xAI, and/or SerpAPI); their handling of that traffic is governed by their respective privacy policies. Nothing is ever sent to the author of this project: no telemetry, no analytics, no account.


**Data use and storage:** Local brand configuration, prompts, scan runs, responses, and cached responses are used only to provide the MCP server features you invoke. They remain in the local SQLite database described above; this project does not operate an account service or collect telemetry.

**Third-party processing:** Prompt and scan traffic is sent only to the AI providers you explicitly configure. Those providers process and retain that traffic under their own privacy policies; the project author does not receive copies of it. Independent Grok and Perplexity Agent API scans use `store:false` to avoid later response retrieval. This is **not** Zero Data Retention: Perplexity may still persist response state, and xAI separately documents default 30-day abuse-audit retention.

**Retention and deletion:** Local data remains on your machine until you delete the SQLite database (or the custom `DIGESTSEO_DB_PATH` you configured). Removing that local database removes mcp-geo's stored local history and cache. Provider-side retention is controlled by each configured provider.

**Contact:** Privacy questions about mcp-geo can be sent to `info@tomiseregi.si`.

---

## License

[MIT](./LICENSE).

Built and maintained by [Tomi Šeregi](https://tomiseregi.si).

---

## Changelog

See [CHANGELOG.md](https://github.com/AKzar1el/mcp-geo/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md) for the full version history.

### [0.3.2] — July 27, 2026

- Published `@digestseo/mcp-geo` with synchronized Worker, MCP Registry, and MCPB metadata.
- Hosted `visibility.*` tool namespaces with typed input/output schemas; local stdio names remain flat.
- Dedicated `mcp-geo-db` D1 configuration and Cursor/Claude Code plugin metadata.
- Patched production dependency pins.

### [0.3.0] — July 2026

- Local stdio CLI on npm (`npx -y @digestseo/mcp-geo`) with SQLite storage and inline engine runs.
- Local brand-management tools: `track_brand`, `list_brands`, `generate_prompts`.
- Runtime-agnostic core shared by Worker and CLI; D1 + better-sqlite3 `Db` adapters.
- MCP Registry `server.json`, MCPB desktop extension, Dockerfile, `llms-install.md`.

### [0.2.1] — June 2026

- Optional `CONNECT_SECRET` gate on the OAuth connect flow.
- Word-boundary brand/competitor matching; exact-domain-or-subdomain linked-citation checks.
- Per-brand `aliases` and `exclude_terms` (migration 0005) for homograph brands like Monday/Notion.
- `visibility.history` includes partial runs and drops fully-failed runs.
- CI workflow (typecheck + unit tests) and a pure-function unit test suite.
- Docs recommend OpenAI + Anthropic as the starting engine pair.
- Constant-time secret comparison.

### [0.2.0] — May 2026

- Per-engine HTTP fan-out via `env.SELF` service binding (one worker invocation per engine, dodges Cloudflare's 1042 self-call guard).
- `status` + `error_message` columns on `prompt_responses` — failed engine calls are now explicit rows, no more `ERROR:` strings in `raw_response`.
- `INSERT OR IGNORE` on the runs row inside `/admin/run-engine` (handles D1 cross-region replication lag without dropping prompt_responses to FK violations).
- Bulk D1 batch in each engine's `runLive` (~26 subrequests/invocation instead of ~89; full 20-prompt runs now fit under the free-plan cap).
- `getLatestCompletedRun` anchored on `EXISTS(ok rows)`; partially-finished runs still show their data.
- New `POST /admin/cleanup-failed-runs` admin route.

### [0.1.1] — May 2026

- Removed the unreliable bash setup script. Manual install via SETUP.md is now the canonical path.

### [0.1.0] — May 2026

- Initial public release.
- 5-engine support: ChatGPT, Claude, Perplexity, Gemini, Google AI Overviews.
- 6 MCP tools.
- Engines opt-in based on which API keys you provide.
- Cloudflare Cron Trigger for auto-refresh.

repository.description: Open source (AGPL-3.0) evidence-grounded repository audit CLI - deterministic scanner, MCP server, live dashboard, and a GitHub Action that posts PR diffs.
repository.name: Aletheore
repository.readme:
Understand your code. Trace the impact of a change.

Scan a repository into structured evidence, inspect its dependencies and ownership, and give coding agents and PR reviews concrete source context.

Run locally · Watch the walkthrough · Explore the evidence

## See the workflow ![Scan → Evidence graph → Coding agent → PR review](assets/readme-workflow.svg) [Watch the 95-second developer walkthrough →](https://www.aletheore.com/#walkthrough) https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/91b58344-d5b7-4be5-b71f-32f1da8499ed With background music and on-screen explanations. Follow a scan of Aletheore's own CLI source, inspect dependencies and related tests, then see how the evidence connects to MCP and PR review. The walkthrough separates captured local output from explanations of hosted features. ## Quickstart Requires **Python 3.11–3.14** and [pipx](https://pipx.pypa.io/latest/how-to/install-pipx.html). Run these commands from a repository you want to inspect: ```bash pipx install aletheore aletheore scan . aletheore query hotspots aletheore dashboard . ``` Open the dashboard at the local URL printed in your terminal. The scan writes `.aletheore/air.json`, a compact `.aletheore/air.toon`, and history snapshots. The deterministic scanner does not call an LLM. Local scanning and structural queries need no Aletheore account or model API key. Registry lookups and optional scanner integrations can use the network; see [Data and network behavior](#data-and-network-behavior). Already installed? Update with `pipx upgrade aletheore`. For a virtual environment or source installation, see the [setup guide](src/README.md#setup). ### Try the built-in demo ```bash aletheore demo ``` The demo creates a small synthetic Python repository with local Git history and runs the real scanner to build reusable evidence, retrieve source, trace imports, and execute a local MCP tool call. In a terminal, arrow-key menus guide one screen at a time, with actions to open the sample dashboard or try your own repository. Use `aletheore demo --plain` for a printable report; piped output also runs without prompts. You can also select **Take the guided demo** from the `aletheore` home menu. Tests are suggested, not executed. Git must be installed; no account, model, or repository clone is needed. The sample and evidence remain in a temporary directory for follow-up queries and the dashboard. Delete that directory when finished. ## See the evidence ### Explore a repository's dependencies [![Local Aletheore dashboard showing the dependency graph of its CLI source](assets/readme-dependencies.png)](assets/readme-dependencies.png) A real local scan of Aletheore's CLI source. Hover modules in the dashboard to explore resolved imports. Security checks were disabled for this capture; graph nodes do not represent a clean security verdict. ### Read a finding where you review code [![Aletheore bot finding on GitHub PR 1128, describing a count-parsing behavior regression](assets/readme-pr-finding.png)](https://github.com/Aletheore/Aletheore/pull/1128) An actual bot comment on [PR #1128](https://github.com/Aletheore/Aletheore/pull/1128). The screenshot shows the review surface; a finding remains something to investigate. ### Explore AIRview [![AIRview public demo showing connected Aletheore modules and their import relationships](assets/readme-airview.png)](https://www.aletheore.com/#live-title) The public AIRview demo, captured from the website using Aletheore's own module graph. [Try the interactive version](https://www.aletheore.com/#live-title) to drag modules and trace imports. This is the public demo rather than an authenticated hosted workspace. ## Start with a question Run a scan first. Replace the example paths and symbol with names from your repository. | What you need to know | Command | | --- | --- | | Where is a function defined? | `aletheore locate find_ownership` | | Who imports this file, directly or indirectly? | `aletheore dependents src/example.py` | | Where is this symbol referenced? | `aletheore usages parse_config` | | Which tests are related to this file? | `aletheore tests-for src/example.py` | | Which files change frequently? | `aletheore query hotspots` | | Who has contributed to a file? | `aletheore query ownership src/example.py` | | Which endpoints are mapped? | `aletheore query endpoints` | | Which secret findings need review? | `aletheore query secrets` | | Are there circular imports? | `aletheore cycles` | `dependents` follows resolved import edges. `tests-for` identifies candidates from import relationships and naming conventions; it does not execute tests or establish coverage. Ownership reflects Git history, rather than an assignment of responsibility. Use `aletheore query` to list available query kinds and `aletheore COMMAND --help` for options. ## Give your coding agent repository evidence ```bash aletheore mcp-install . --target cursor ``` This writes client configuration so Cursor can launch the repository's MCP server. Restart or reload the client as needed. Other supported targets include Claude Code, VS Code, Kiro, Opencode, Antigravity, Codex CLI, and Claude Desktop; list the current options with `aletheore mcp-install --help`. An agent can inspect symbols, imports, dependents, owners, endpoints, and related evidence without starting each investigation from an unstructured repository dump. For example, ask your agent: > Before changing this function, use Aletheore to locate its definition, inspect its > references and import dependents, and identify candidate tests. Cite the evidence and > distinguish resolved relationships from uncertainty. For clients you configure manually, the server command is `aletheore mcp .`. Optional AI answering, semantic indexing, and external tools have their own setup and network requirements. See the [MCP guide](src/README.md#aletheore-mcp-path). ## Check and undo what an agent changes Shield is a local safety net for AI-written changes in a Git repository. It makes no model call. ```bash pipx install aletheore # or: pip install aletheore aletheore shield ``` `aletheore shield` shows every change it plans, with a diff for each file, then waits. Type `yes` to set it up. Nothing is written before that. Once Shield is on, the same command shows its status. The explicit forms are `aletheore shield setup` and `aletheore shield status`; setup run again shows only what needs updating. Setup changes: - `.claude/settings.local.json`: Claude Code hooks for four events (before an edit, after an edit, end of turn, end of session), each the Python interpreter plus arguments, so no shell quoting is involved. This file is personal and is not committed. Entries an earlier Shield wrote as one shell-command string are noted by `aletheore shield status`; `aletheore shield setup` updates them in place. - The Git `pre-commit` hook: a marked block that prints Shield's report and never fails the commit. Tools that generate Git hooks (pre-commit, lefthook, husky) can overwrite that block; `aletheore shield status` then notes that the Git hook is missing, and `aletheore shield setup` puts it back. - `.git/info/exclude`: a marked block that keeps Shield's files out of `git status`. `.gitignore` is not touched. - `.aletheore/shield/config.json`, and private records under the Git directory. - A first local scan into `.aletheore/`, if the repository has no evidence yet. What it does: - **Guard.** After edits, at the end of a turn and at commit, it reports new or suspicious dependencies (checked against PyPI and npm), files the change reaches and candidate tests, signature changes (stated per file that imports the module, not per call site), and new secrets and import cycles. Vulnerability and layer-convention findings appear only when the evidence came from a full `aletheore scan`. - **Checkpoints.** Before an agent edits, Shield saves the working tree as a Git commit under `refs/aletheore/checkpoints/`. Your branches, index and stash are not touched. Put files back with `aletheore shield undo`; it saves a safety checkpoint first and never deletes a file. - **Receipts.** At the end of a session, `.aletheore/shield/receipts/` gets a file listing what changed and what the guard found. What it does not do: - It never blocks a commit or an agent turn. - It does not run the candidate tests. Dependency and signature checks work at the import level, not the call level. - Only PyPI and npm are checked. Any other dependency is reported as "not checked". - It does not refresh stale scan evidence inline; checks that need fresh evidence say they were skipped. - Each hook has a time limit. Anything the guard could not finish in time is listed as not checked, never reported as a finding. Measured on two 9,400-file repositories: about 0.6 s per hook on a copy of this repository and 0.45-0.8 s on a generated one (1.2-1.3 s at session end on both). Registry lookups send only the package name to `pypi.org` or `registry.npmjs.org`, never versions, paths or source. They run only at turn end, at commit and in `aletheore shield check`. Turn them off with `ALETHEORE_SHIELD_OFFLINE=1` or `"registry_lookups": false` in `.aletheore/shield/config.json`. With lookups on, the answers are cached in `~/.cache/aletheore/shield-registry-cache.json` (under your user profile on Windows), outside the repository; `off --purge` leaves that file. Checkpoint refs are local; `git push --mirror` pushes every ref including them, so avoid it or delete the refs first. Undo writes files the way `git checkout` would, following your line-ending and filter settings. `aletheore shield off` removes the hooks, config and marked blocks and keeps checkpoints and receipts; `--purge` deletes those too. Scan evidence in `.aletheore/` stays, and so does a one-line git exclude for it until you delete `.aletheore/` and run `off` again. Shield targets macOS, Linux and Windows; CI runs the unit tests and a CLI smoke test of setup, the four hooks and `off` on all three. It has not been run against a real Claude Code session on Windows. See the [command reference](src/README.md#aletheore-shield) for options, limits and exit codes. ## What you can use | Surface | Purpose | Start here | | --- | --- | --- | | Local CLI | Scan, locate code, inspect risks, and compare evidence | `aletheore scan .` | | Local dashboard | Explore dependency and cluster graphs and scan history | `aletheore dashboard .` | | MCP server | Let a coding agent query repository evidence | `aletheore mcp-install --help` | | AI audit | Generate a report using a configured coding-agent CLI or API provider | `aletheore audit --help` | | Hallbook | Search the bundled coding-agent skill catalog | `aletheore hallbook search "code review"` | | Shield | Check and undo what a coding agent changes in a Git repository | `aletheore shield` | | Agent context tools | Inspect tool overhead and local context savings | `aletheore tokens meter` | | GitHub Action | Report new and resolved findings between a PR's base and head | [Action setup](#run-in-github-actions) | | Hosted GitHub App | Run PR reviews and use managed repository features | [Install the app](https://github.com/apps/aletheore/installations/new) | Hallbook skills have individual instructions, dependencies, and licenses; review a skill before installing or executing it. Token auditing can invoke your configured agent; context profiles are optional and change which tools that agent can access. ## Review changes in GitHub The hosted GitHub App adds PR reviews, managed audits, AIRview architecture pages, AI-marked symbol documentation, and endpoint monitoring with source context. Availability depends on the selected plan. Free AI reviews are globally rate-limited and subject to availability. See [current plans and limits](https://www.aletheore.com/pricing) rather than relying on a price copied into this README. [Install the Aletheore GitHub App](https://github.com/apps/aletheore/installations/new) and choose the repositories to connect. ### Run in GitHub Actions
GitHub Actions workflow and execution notes For a deterministic PR diff in your own workflow: ```yaml name: Aletheore on: [pull_request] permissions: contents: read pull-requests: write jobs: evidence: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - uses: Aletheore/Aletheore@v0.13.0 with: fail-on-new-secrets: true ``` The Action scans both refs and reports new/resolved secrets, dependency vulnerabilities, and layer-convention violations. It runs `scan` and `diff`, rather than an AI audit. The example pins an existing release; review and pin a commit SHA for your own deployment policy. Fork PRs can have read-only tokens: comment posting may be unavailable even when analysis succeeds. See [Action inputs](action.yml) and the [CLI reference](src/README.md).
## What the scanner understands

Dependency graph support, with language-specific resolution limits:

Language support, available evidence, and analysis limits Dependency graphs support **Python, JavaScript/JSX, TypeScript/TSX, Go, Rust, Java, Kotlin, Ruby, PHP, C, C++, C#, and Swift**, with language-specific resolution limits. Secrets and Git analysis can still apply to other source files. Dependency checks depend on supported manifests, resolved versions, and registry coverage. The evidence can include imports, symbols, clusters, Git ownership and activity, secret findings, dependency vulnerabilities and licenses, static analysis, endpoints, database schema, infrastructure, and error handling. Some checks depend on installed external scanners or explicit configuration. Missing tools and unsupported analysis must be distinguished from a clean result. Static evidence is a starting point for investigation. Dynamic dispatch, runtime configuration, external services, and unresolved imports can leave gaps. A source citation makes a claim inspectable; it does not by itself prove that a bug exists or that a change is safe. Read [resolution details and configuration](src/README.md) for the limits that apply to your language.
## Data and network behavior Local scans build evidence on your machine. Enabled registry checks, optional integrations, crash reporting, and AI features have their own network behavior.
Network requests, crash reporting, and offline scan flags The local deterministic scan builds evidence on your machine. Its network behavior depends on enabled checks and integrations: - Dependency vulnerability and license checks contact OSV and package registries. - Semgrep can fetch rules and send its own metrics; optional integrations such as SonarQube have separate submission behavior. - CLI startup can check PyPI for updates. Set `ALETHEORE_NO_UPDATE_CHECK=1` to disable that check. - Crash reporting is enabled by default and can be disabled with `aletheore config crash-reporting off` or `ALETHEORE_CRASH_REPORTING=0`. - AI audits, hosted features, and configured semantic services send the context required by the selected workflow to their configured services. Local evidence can contain sensitive metadata or source excerpts; review it before sharing. Before scanning, inspect potential traffic for the resolved configuration: ```bash aletheore scan . --explain-network ``` This prints the conditional network paths and exits without scanning. It is an explanation of configured behavior, rather than a firewall or packet trace. To skip registry and static-scanner checks for a local scan: ```bash aletheore scan . --no-check-vulnerabilities --no-check-licenses --no-check-static-analysis ``` These scan flags do not configure every other command or service. Review [CLI configuration and crash reporting](src/README.md#crash-reporting), [security information](SECURITY.md), and the hosted [privacy policy](https://www.aletheore.com/privacy) for the workflow you choose.
## Evidence and benchmarks Explore [published scan examples](https://www.aletheore.com/dogfooding) and [benchmarks with methodology and limits](https://www.aletheore.com/benchmarks). The separate [benchmark repository](https://github.com/Aletheore/aletheore-benchmarks) contains the PR-review evaluation harness. Results depend on repository, task, model, and sample; they do not guarantee the same result on your code. ## Contribute or get help - [Report a bug or request a feature](https://github.com/Aletheore/Aletheore/issues). - Read [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) to work on the project. - Use [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md) for vulnerability reports. - [Sponsor development](https://github.com/sponsors/ArihantK15).

sampled_files.README.md:
Understand your code. Trace the impact of a change.

Scan a repository into structured evidence, inspect its dependencies and ownership, and give coding agents and PR reviews concrete source context.

Run locally · Watch the walkthrough · Explore the evidence

## See the workflow ![Scan → Evidence graph → Coding agent → PR review](assets/readme-workflow.svg) [Watch the 95-second developer walkthrough →](https://www.aletheore.com/#walkthrough) https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/91b58344-d5b7-4be5-b71f-32f1da8499ed With background music and on-screen explanations. Follow a scan of Aletheore's own CLI source, inspect dependencies and related tests, then see how the evidence connects to MCP and PR review. The walkthrough separates captured local output from explanations of hosted features. ## Quickstart Requires **Python 3.11–3.14** and [pipx](https://pipx.pypa.io/latest/how-to/install-pipx.html). Run these commands from a repository you want to inspect: ```bash pipx install aletheore aletheore scan . aletheore query hotspots aletheore dashboard . ``` Open the dashboard at the local URL printed in your terminal. The scan writes `.aletheore/air.json`, a compact `.aletheore/air.toon`, and history snapshots. The deterministic scanner does not call an LLM. Local scanning and structural queries need no Aletheore account or model API key. Registry lookups and optional scanner integrations can use the network; see [Data and network behavior](#data-and-network-behavior). Already installed? Update with `pipx upgrade aletheore`. For a virtual environment or source installation, see the [setup guide](src/README.md#setup). ### Try the built-in demo ```bash aletheore demo ``` The demo creates a small synthetic Python repository with local Git history and runs the real scanner to build reusable evidence, retrieve source, trace imports, and execute a local MCP tool call. In a terminal, arrow-key menus guide one screen at a time, with actions to open the sample dashboard or try your own repository. Use `aletheore demo --plain` for a printable report; piped output also runs without prompts. You can also select **Take the guided demo** from the `aletheore` home menu. Tests are suggested, not executed. Git must be installed; no account, model, or repository clone is needed. The sample and evidence remain in a temporary directory for follow-up queries and the dashboard. Delete that directory when finished. ## See the evidence ### Explore a repository's dependencies [![Local Aletheore dashboard showing the dependency graph of its CLI source](assets/readme-dependencies.png)](assets/readme-dependencies.png) A real local scan of Aletheore's CLI source. Hover modules in the dashboard to explore resolved imports. Security checks were disabled for this capture; graph nodes do not represent a clean security verdict. ### Read a finding where you review code [![Aletheore bot finding on GitHub PR 1128, describing a count-parsing behavior regression](assets/readme-pr-finding.png)](https://github.com/Aletheore/Aletheore/pull/1128) An actual bot comment on [PR #1128](https://github.com/Aletheore/Aletheore/pull/1128). The screenshot shows the review surface; a finding remains something to investigate. ### Explore AIRview [![AIRview public demo showing connected Aletheore modules and their import relationships](assets/readme-airview.png)](https://www.aletheore.com/#live-title) The public AIRview demo, captured from the website using Aletheore's own module graph. [Try the interactive version](https://www.aletheore.com/#live-title) to drag modules and trace imports. This is the public demo rather than an authenticated hosted workspace. ## Start with a question Run a scan first. Replace the example paths and symbol with names from your repository. | What you need to know | Command | | --- | --- | | Where is a function defined? | `aletheore locate find_ownership` | | Who imports this file, directly or indirectly? | `aletheore dependents src/example.py` | | Where is this symbol referenced? | `aletheore usages parse_config` | | Which tests are related to this file? | `aletheore tests-for src/example.py` | | Which files change frequently? | `aletheore query hotspots` | | Who has contributed to a file? | `aletheore query ownership src/example.py` | | Which endpoints are mapped? | `aletheore query endpoints` | | Which secret findings need review? | `aletheore query secrets` | | Are there circular imports? | `aletheore cycles` | `dependents` follows resolved import edges. `tests-for` identifies candidates from import relationships and naming conventions; it does not execute tests or establish coverage. Ownership reflects Git history, rather than an assignment of responsibility. Use `aletheore query` to list available query kinds and `aletheore COMMAND --help` for options. ## Give your coding agent repository evidence ```bash aletheore mcp-install . --target cursor ``` This writes client configuration so Cursor can launch the repository's MCP server. Restart or reload the client as needed. Other supported targets include Claude Code, VS Code, Kiro, Opencode, Antigravity, Codex CLI, and Claude Desktop; list the current options with `aletheore mcp-install --help`. An agent can inspect symbols, imports, dependents, owners, endpoints, and related evidence without starting each investigation from an unstructured repository dump. For example, ask your agent: > Before changing this function, use Aletheore to locate its definition, inspect its > references and import dependents, and identify candidate tests. Cite the evidence and > distinguish resolved relationships from uncertainty. For clients you configure manually, the server command is `aletheore mcp .`. Optional AI answering, semantic indexing, and external tools have their own setup and network requirements. See the [MCP guide](src/README.md#aletheore-mcp-path). ## Check and undo what an agent changes Shield is a local safety net for AI-written changes in a Git repository. It makes no model call. ```bash pipx install aletheore # or: pip install aletheore aletheore shield ``` `aletheore shield` shows every change it plans, with a diff for each file, then waits. Type `yes` to set it up. Nothing is written before that. Once Shield is on, the same command shows its status. The explicit forms are `aletheore shield setup` and `aletheore shield status`; setup run again shows only what needs updating. Setup changes: - `.claude/settings.local.json`: Claude Code hooks for four events (before an edit, after an edit, end of turn, end of session), each the Python interpreter plus arguments, so no shell quoting is involved. This file is personal and is not committed. Entries an earlier Shield wrote as one shell-command string are noted by `aletheore shield status`; `aletheore shield setup` updates them in place. - The Git `pre-commit` hook: a marked block that prints Shield's report and never fails the commit. Tools that generate Git hooks (pre-commit, lefthook, husky) can overwrite that block; `aletheore shield status` then notes that the Git hook is missing, and `aletheore shield setup` puts it back. - `.git/info/exclude`: a marked block that keeps Shield's files out of `git status`. `.gitignore` is not touched. - `.aletheore/shield/config.json`, and private records under the Git directory. - A first local scan into `.aletheore/`, if the repository has no evidence yet. What it does: - **Guard.** After edits, at the end of a turn and at commit, it reports new or suspicious dependencies (checked against PyPI and npm), files the change reaches and candidate tests, signature changes (stated per file that imports the module, not per call site), and new secrets and import cycles. Vulnerability and layer-convention findings appear only when the evidence came from a full `aletheore scan`. - **Checkpoints.** Before an agent edits, Shield saves the working tree as a Git commit under `refs/aletheore/checkpoints/`. Your branches, index and stash are not touched. Put files back with `aletheore shield undo`; it saves a safety checkpoint first and never deletes a file. - **Receipts.** At the end of a session, `.aletheore/shield/receipts/` gets a file listing what changed and what the guard found. What it does not do: - It never blocks a commit or an agent turn. - It does not run the candidate tests. Dependency and signature checks work at the import level, not the call level. - Only PyPI and npm are checked. Any other dependency is reported as "not checked". - It does not refresh stale scan evidence inline; checks that need fresh evidence say they were skipped. - Each hook has a time limit. Anything the guard could not finish in time is listed as not checked, never reported as a finding. Measured on two 9,400-file repositories: about 0.6 s per hook on a copy of this repository and 0.45-0.8 s on a generated one (1.2-1.3 s at session end on both). Registry lookups send only the package name to `pypi.org` or `registry.npmjs.org`, never versions, paths or source. They run only at turn end, at commit and in `aletheore shield check`. Turn them off with `ALETHEORE_SHIELD_OFFLINE=1` or `"registry_lookups": false` in `.aletheore/shield/config.json`. With lookups on, the answers are cached in `~/.cache/aletheore/shield-registry-cache.json` (under your user profile on Windows), outside the repository; `off --purge` leaves that file. Checkpoint refs are local; `git push --mirror` pushes every ref including them, so avoid it or delete the refs first. Undo writes files the way `git checkout` would, following your line-ending and filter settings. `aletheore shield off` removes the hooks, config and marked blocks and keeps checkpoints and receipts; `--purge` deletes those too. Scan evidence in `.aletheore/` stays, and so does a one-line git exclude for it until you delete `.aletheore/` and run `off` again. Shield targets macOS, Linux and Windows; CI runs the unit tests and a CLI smoke test of setup, the four hooks and `off` on all three. It has not been run against a real Claude Code session on Windows. See the [command reference](src/README.md#aletheore-shield) for options, limits and exit codes. ## What you can use | Surface | Purpose | Start here | | --- | --- | --- | | Local CLI | Scan, locate code, inspect risks, and compare evidence | `aletheore scan .` | | Local dashboard | Explore dependency and cluster graphs and scan history | `aletheore dashboard .` | | MCP server | Let a coding agent query repository evidence | `aletheore mcp-install --help` | | AI audit | Generate a report using a configured coding-agent CLI or API provider | `aletheore audit --help` | | Hallbook | Search the bundled coding-agent skill catalog | `aletheore hallbook search "code review"` | | Shield | Check and undo what a coding agent changes in a Git repository | `aletheore shield` | | Agent context tools | Inspect tool overhead and local context savings | `aletheore tokens meter` | | GitHub Action | Report new and resolved findings between a PR's base and head | [Action setup](#run-in-github-actions) | | Hosted GitHub App | Run PR reviews and use managed repository features | [Install the app](https://github.com/apps/aletheore/installations/new) | Hallbook skills have individual instructions, dependencies, and licenses; review a skill before installing or executing it. Token auditing can invoke your configured agent; context profiles are optional and change which tools that agent can access. ## Review changes in GitHub The hosted GitHub App adds PR reviews, managed audits, AIRview architecture pages, AI-marked symbol documentation, and endpoint monitoring with source context. Availability depends on the selected plan. Free AI reviews are globally rate-limited and subject to availability. See [current plans and limits](https://www.aletheore.com/pricing) rather than relying on a price copied into this README. [Install the Aletheore GitHub App](https://github.com/apps/aletheore/installations/new) and choose the repositories to connect. ### Run in GitHub Actions
GitHub Actions workflow and execution notes For a deterministic PR diff in your own workflow: ```yaml name: Aletheore on: [pull_request] permissions: contents: read pull-requests: write jobs: evidence: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - uses: Aletheore/Aletheore@v0.13.0 with: fail-on-new-secrets: true ``` The Action scans both refs and reports new/resolved secrets, dependency vulnerabilities, and layer-convention violations. It runs `scan` and `diff`, rather than an AI audit. The example pins an existing release; review and pin a commit SHA for your own deployment policy. Fork PRs can have read-only tokens: comment posting may be unavailable even when analysis succeeds. See [Action inputs](action.yml) and the [CLI reference](src/README.md).
## What the scanner understands

Dependency graph support, with language-specific resolution limits:

Language support, available evidence, and analysis limits Dependency graphs support **Python, JavaScript/JSX, TypeScript/TSX, Go, Rust, Java, Kotlin, Ruby, PHP, C, C++, C#, and Swift**, with language-specific resolution limits. Secrets and Git analysis can still apply to other source files. Dependency checks depend on supported manifests, resolved versions, and registry coverage. The evidence can include imports, symbols, clusters, Git ownership and activity, secret findings, dependency vulnerabilities and licenses, static analysis, endpoints, database schema, infrastructure, and error handling. Some checks depend on installed external scanners or explicit configuration. Missing tools and unsupported analysis must be distinguished from a clean result. Static evidence is a starting point for investigation. Dynamic dispatch, runtime configuration, external services, and unresolved imports can leave gaps. A source citation makes a claim inspectable; it does not by itself prove that a bug exists or that a change is safe. Read [resolution details and configuration](src/README.md) for the limits that apply to your language.
## Data and network behavior Local scans build evidence on your machine. Enabled registry checks, optional integrations, crash reporting, and AI features have their own network behavior.
Network requests, crash reporting, and offline scan flags The local deterministic scan builds evidence on your machine. Its network behavior depends on enabled checks and integrations: - Dependency vulnerability and license checks contact OSV and package registries. - Semgrep can fetch rules and send its own metrics; optional integrations such as SonarQube have separate submission behavior. - CLI startup can check PyPI for updates. Set `ALETHEORE_NO_UPDATE_CHECK=1` to disable that check. - Crash reporting is enabled by default and can be disabled with `aletheore config crash-reporting off` or `ALETHEORE_CRASH_REPORTING=0`. - AI audits, hosted features, and configured semantic services send the context required by the selected workflow to their configured services. Local evidence can contain sensitive metadata or source excerpts; review it before sharing. Before scanning, inspect potential traffic for the resolved configuration: ```bash aletheore scan . --explain-network ``` This prints the conditional network paths and exits without scanning. It is an explanation of configured behavior, rather than a firewall or packet trace. To skip registry and static-scanner checks for a local scan: ```bash aletheore scan . --no-check-vulnerabilities --no-check-licenses --no-check-static-analysis ``` These scan flags do not configure every other command or service. Review [CLI configuration and crash reporting](src/README.md#crash-reporting), [security information](SECURITY.md), and the hosted [privacy policy](https://www.aletheore.com/privacy) for the workflow you choose.
## Evidence and benchmarks Explore [published scan examples](https://www.aletheore.com/dogfooding) and [benchmarks with methodology and limits](https://www.aletheore.com/benchmarks). The separate [benchmark repository](https://github.com/Aletheore/aletheore-benchmarks) contains the PR-review evaluation harness. Results depend on repository, task, model, and sample; they do not guarantee the same result on your code. ## Contribute or get help - [Report a bug or request a feature](https://github.com/Aletheore/Aletheore/issues). - Read [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) to work on the project. - Use [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md) for vulnerability reports. - [Sponsor development](https://github.com/sponsors/ArihantK15).

repository.description: The ultimate harness for coding agents and beyond. All your agents. All your machines. One command center. Start with code, then follow your curiosity and build across disciplines: CAD, circuits, robots, games and music.
repository.name: openharness
repository.readme:
Harness like a boss.

The ultimate harness for coding agents and beyond.
Claude Code at work. Codex at home. Hermes in the cloud. One command center.
Start with code. Then follow your curiosity and build across disciplines: CAD, circuits, robots, games and music.

Download · How it works · Beyond code · Harnesses · Device

### Every agent, side by side Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, OpenCode, Devin, Amp, Copilot and seven more.

### Every machine, side by side Your laptop, home server and GPU box in one window. Link each one with a password. No SSH keys. No Tailscale. No port forwarding.

### Keyboard first ⌘P finds any harness on any machine. ⇧⌘I jumps to the harness waiting on you. ⌘D splits. Every key remaps.

### End-to-end encrypted Code, keys and keystrokes are sealed on your machine. The relay forwards bytes it can't read.

### Fast and light A native app, not Electron. Close it and your agents keep working. Idle measurements on an M2 Max: - **⌘N, ⌘O, ⌘T UI:** 11–13 ms median, 15–18 ms p95. - **Local terminal echo:** 1.1 ms median, 7.2 ms p95, excluding UI rendering. - **Desktop resources:** ~0.1% of one CPU core and 304 MiB, including terminal rendering and scrollback; agent CLIs and the daemon are excluded. Desktop results use a Release fixture with 16 terminals and 1,000 scrollback lines each. See the [workflow and resource benchmarks](docs/performance/2026-09-23-core-experiences.md) and [remote P2P, TURN and relay results](docs/performance/2026-09-23-transport-routes.md) for workloads, slow tails, connection failures and raw data. ### Built the way developers work - **Real terminals.** Every agent runs in its own tmux pane. Scrollback, colors and keys just work. - **Your CLIs, as they are.** Harness never wraps an agent. It reads transcripts and uses the vendor's own hooks. - **A worktree per harness.** Start an agent on its own branch. Your working copy stays clean. - **Remap every key.** One JSONC file, reloaded on save. Chords up to four strokes. - **Local models.** Run open-weight models on your own machines with Grid, Ollama, MLX-LM and vLLM. - **Bytes, not pixels.** Remote terminals stream text peer to peer. No remote desktop. - **Open source, all of it.** App, CLI, daemon, relay and device, in this repo. ## How it works In the workspace, a **harness** is one running session of an agent such as Codex or Claude Code, with its own conversation and working context. A **tab** groups harnesses. Use **New Harness** to start one and **New Tab** to group work. Harnesses in the same tab can message each other with `harness send`: **Agent Messages**, an experiment of your account, off by default and turned on in Settings ▸ Experimental. The Store offers **harnesses** with instructions, tools, and optional viewers for specific crafts. Install a harness, then start it in your workspace. See the [Naming System](docs/naming-system.md) for the complete naming rules. One daemon per machine runs your agents in tmux. It dials out, so no machine opens a port. ```mermaid flowchart LR subgraph laptop["Your laptop"] app["Harness app"] -- loopback --> d1["daemon"] d1 --> a1["tmux · Claude Code · Codex"] end subgraph box["Your GPU box"] d2["daemon"] --> a2["tmux · OpenCode · Hermes"] end device["Harness device"] -- USB --> d1 d1 <-. "direct WebRTC" .-> d2 d1 <-- "ciphertext" --> relay["Harness relay · no keys"] relay <-- "ciphertext" --> d2 ``` Every path is sealed end to end: ChaCha20-Poly1305, X25519 session keys, pinned Ed25519 identities. Harness picks the best path on its own. **Direct.** A WebRTC channel between your machines. No server in the path.

**Through Cloudflare.** When a firewall blocks the direct path, the same encrypted channel runs over Cloudflare's TURN network. Harness keeps trying for a direct path.

**Through our relay.** A fallback while WebRTC negotiates. The relay holds no keys and forwards ciphertext.

The [architecture guide](docs/architecture.md) has the details. ## Get started **[Download the app](https://harness.autonomous.ai/desktop?utm_source=github&utm_medium=readme)** for macOS or Linux. Add a machine. Run this on it, then **Machines → Link Machine** in the app: ```bash curl -fsSL https://harness.autonomous.ai/cli/install.sh | bash harness login harness remote-password set harness start ``` **In a terminal:** the same line installs `hn` — tmux's keys and your `~/.tmux.conf`, with every harness on every machine ([hn](tui/README.md)). The first time, `hn` signs in and connects the computer: ```bash curl -fsSL https://harness.autonomous.ai/cli/install.sh | bash hn ``` **For agents:** Claude Code and Codex can start, wait for and read other harnesses with the `harness` skill ([harness.autonomous.ai/agents](https://harness.autonomous.ai/agents), which has the Codex lines too): ```bash claude plugin marketplace add autonomous-ai/openharness --sparse .claude-plugin plugins claude plugin install harness@openharness ```
Build from source Needs Node.js 20+, tmux, Xcode and Flutter 3.47+ / Dart 3.13+: ```bash git clone https://github.com/autonomous-ai/openharness.git cd openharness (cd cli && npm ci) make install-cli cd desktop flutter config --enable-swift-package-manager flutter pub get flutter run -d macos ``` `make install-cli` installs this checkout's CLI and restarts the local daemon. See the [development guide](docs/development.md).
## Beyond code: Build across disciplines > “World-class entrepreneurs are polymaths.” — [Peter Thiel](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=h10kXgTdhNU&t=811s) Coding agents can build far more than software. Give one a harness and it works with the real tools of a craft. You steer in a live viewer. Every clip below is a real session. ### Beyond code: Design **[Blender](store/agents/blender/).** Ask for a lamp and the sliders that matter. Turn them and Blender rebuilds the geometry. Keep the versions you love.

### Beyond code: Circuits **[CircuitJS](store/agents/circuitjs/).** Build a filter. Change one resistor. Overlay the new trace, measure the difference and keep both.

### Beyond code: Robotics **[MuJoCo](store/agents/mujoco/).** Pin a moment in a robot's run. Shove it with 100 N. Watch two futures split.

### Beyond code: Games **[Godogen](store/agents/godogen/).** Your agent makes a playable game. Miss a jump, rewind, try again. Pin the moment so the agent sees what you mean.

### Beyond code: Music **[Strudel](store/agents/strudel/).** The track is code you can perform. Bring voices in and out, mark the good parts, keep the WAV. [Hear it](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/a3d4381b-5f55-406c-9d68-330cd8792fc5).

### Beyond code: Chemistry **[RDKit](store/agents/rdkit/).** Turn a bond and watch the molecule move. Follow the real energy curve. Keep the pose worth a closer look.

### Beyond code: Documents **[Typst](store/agents/typst/).** Your agent writes a real PDF. Circle a detail, quote a line, leave a note. The next draft answers it.

## Domain-specific harnesses (DSH) Code is the common medium. Geometry scripts make parts. Netlists make boards. Animation code makes film. A **domain-specific harness** turns a coding agent into a specialist. It brings the craft's instructions and skills, a pinned toolchain, a project template, checks and a **live viewer**. You chat on one side. The board, the part or the game takes shape on the other. The agent does the reasoning. The harness supplies the tools and the view. It's a folder with a `harness.json`, so adding a craft never touches the app. ### 49 harnesses in the Store | Category | Agents and harnesses | |---|---| | **Coding** | [Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, OpenCode, Pi, Hermes, Command Code, Devin, Muse Code, Amp, Antigravity, GitHub Copilot, Grok Build, Kilo Code](docs/engines.md), [Machine Monitor](store/agents/machine-monitor/), [Trail of Bits Skills](store/agents/trailofbits-skills/) | | Essentials | [Harness Monitor](store/agents/harness-monitor/), [Memories](store/agents/memories/) | | Design | [Autonomous Workshop](store/agents/autonomous-workshop/), [Blender](store/agents/blender/), [Bonsai MCP](store/agents/bonsai-mcp/), [Creative Direction](store/agents/creative-direction/), [Excalidraw](store/agents/excalidraw/), [FreeCAD](store/agents/freecad/), [Generative Art](store/agents/generative-art/), [OpenSCAD](store/agents/openscad/), [text-to-cad](store/agents/text-to-cad/) | | Engineering | [Autonomous Circuit](store/agents/autonomous-circuit/), [CircuitJS](store/agents/circuitjs/), [Home Assistant](store/agents/home-assistant/), [KiCad](store/agents/kicad/), [Orca Slicer](store/agents/orca-slicer/), [Yosys](store/agents/yosys/) | | Media | [Comfy MCP](store/agents/comfy-mcp/), [Manim](store/agents/manim/), [OpenMontage](store/agents/openmontage/), [Remotion](store/agents/remotion/) | | Music | [Ableton AI](store/agents/ableton-ai/), [JUCE Agent Toolkit](store/agents/juce-agent-toolkit/), [Music Studio](store/agents/music-studio/), [Score](store/agents/score/), [Strudel](store/agents/strudel/) | | Productivity | [Marp](store/agents/marp/), [Typst](store/agents/typst/) | | Science & Data | [autoresearch-mlx](store/agents/autoresearch-mlx/), [Data Studio](store/agents/data-studio/), [Lab Bench](store/agents/lab-bench/), [marimo](store/agents/marimo/), [RDKit](store/agents/rdkit/) | | Simulation | [DimOS](store/agents/dimos/), [Drone Pilot](store/agents/drone-pilot/), [Foam-Agent](store/agents/foam-agent/), [MuJoCo](store/agents/mujoco/), [SimSkill](store/agents/simskill/) | | Games | [Game Master](store/agents/game-master/), [Godogen](store/agents/godogen/), [Phaser](store/agents/phaser/), [Voxel Worlds](store/agents/voxel-worlds/) | | Research | [Roundtable](store/agents/roundtable/) | | Local AI | [MLX-LM](store/agents/mlx-lm/), [Model Manager](store/agents/autonomous-grid/), [Ollama](store/agents/ollama/), [vLLM](store/agents/vllm/) | Upstream open-source tools and original workflows. 10 [shared viewers](store/viewers/) install alongside the harnesses that need them. Unlisted experiments are not shown. ### Build your own The next harness is the one for your craft. Wrap a tool you love or your team's toolchain. It can live here or in your own repo. From this repo: ```json { "spec": 1, "id": "examples/hello-world", "name": "Hello World", "engine": "codex", "workspace": { "template": "template", "marker": "index.html" }, "agent": { "instructions": "AGENTS.md" }, "viewer": { "use": "autonomous/web-viewer" } } ``` ```bash harness dsh install "$PWD/store/viewers/web-viewer" --link cp -R store/examples/hello-world ../my-harness harness dsh check ../my-harness harness dsh install ../my-harness --link ``` Press **⌘N → Hello World** and say hello. The [authoring guide](store/README.md) covers the rest. ## Harness device [**Get a Harness device**](https://www.autonomous.ai/harness-device), or build your own from the files below. The [firmware guide](devices/harness-device/firmware/README.md) lists the supported boards and build commands, and the [hardware guide](devices/harness-device/hardware/README.md) covers the design files.

The optional **Harness device** is a round, always-on display that sits beside your keyboard and shows your agents at a glance: what each one is doing, which one has finished, and which one is waiting on you. Read a question and answer it on the screen, or tap and speak a new task, without switching windows. It is open hardware, all the way down. This repository has everything it takes to build one: | Layer | What's here | |---|---| | [Firmware](devices/harness-device/firmware/) | ESP32-S3, ESP-IDF, a 466 × 466 round AMOLED with touch, microphones and audio. Connects to the host's daemon over USB — no Wi-Fi setup, no account on the device. | | [PCB](devices/harness-device/hardware/pcb/) | The EasyEDA Pro project, the schematic, Gerbers, the bill of materials, and pick-and-place data for assembly. | | [Enclosure](devices/harness-device/hardware/3d/) | STEP for editing and STL for printing: the housing, an iron counterweight base, the USB clamp, and the button. | ## Contribute Make a harness for a tool you love. Improve terminals, engines, the daemon or the relay. Port the firmware. Start with the [contribution guide](CONTRIBUTING.md). [Architecture](docs/architecture.md) · [Product direction (proposal)](docs/product-direction.md) · [Development](docs/development.md) · [Extending](docs/extending.md) · [CLI](docs/cli.md) · [Security](SECURITY.md) · [MIT license](LICENSE); upstream tools keep their own.
