![Olympus: a towering mountain crowned by a celestial palace, surrounded by cyborg gods, AI agents, and lobster adventurers](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jamiezigelbaum/Olympus/main/assets/olympus-banner.png) # ⛰️ Olympus **Your machine, your memory. Keep your private things private.** Olympus keeps your email, files and messages on your own computer and decides, item by item, what each AI may see. ChatGPT, Claude, Grok and any app that speaks MCP can use it, while your private things stay private. On a Mac, and on [Omarchy](https://omarchy.org) and Ubuntu 24.04 LTS Linux. Free and open source. [![version](https://img.shields.io/badge/version-1.4.2-534AB7)](https://github.com/jamiezigelbaum/Olympus/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md) [![license](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-MIT-0F6E56)](https://github.com/jamiezigelbaum/Olympus/blob/main/LICENSE) [![tests](https://img.shields.io/badge/tests-3400%2B%20passing-1D9E75)](https://github.com/jamiezigelbaum/Olympus/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md) [![openclaw](https://img.shields.io/badge/OpenClaw-2026.7.1%2B-378ADD)](https://openclaw.ai) [![runtime](https://img.shields.io/badge/runtime-Bun%20%2B%20TypeScript-B45309)](https://bun.sh) [olympusplugin.ai](https://olympusplugin.ai) · [Get started](#get-started) · [Olympus in ChatGPT](#olympus-for-chatgpt) · [Claude, Grok and other apps](#claude-grok-and-other-apps) · [How it works](#how-it-works) · [Sources](#supported-sources) · [Security model](#the-security-model) · [OpenClaw quickstart](https://github.com/jamiezigelbaum/Olympus/blob/main/docs/QUICKSTART.md) · [Commands](#command-reference) --- > **🤖 Installing this as an AI agent for OpenClaw?** Stop and read > **[INSTALL_FOR_AGENTS.md](INSTALL_FOR_AGENTS.md)** before running any > command — it is the step-by-step runbook you must follow, including > exactly what to tell your operator after each step (your install report > must end with the Step 1→2 invitation, never a bare status line). Managed > `git:`, `clawhub:`, and `npm-pack:` installs intentionally hide their internal > package path; use the installed `olympus` CLI and this packaged runbook rather > than searching OpenClaw's managed storage. **Setting up Olympus for ChatGPT, > Claude or Grok instead?** Follow [Get started](#get-started), not this > runbook. --- Frontier AI models are the smartest, but using them means sending your life to someone else's cloud. Local models keep it home, but they are a step behind, and the best ones need an expensive computer under your desk. Olympus gives you both, on the laptop you already have. Every email, file and message is judged, one by one, as **Personal**, **Private** or **Secret**: on your own computer by default, or by Venice's private models if you choose a Venice-only setup. - **Personal:** ChatGPT, Claude or Grok can read the parts that answer your question, and cite them. - **Private:** only a model on your computer reads it (or Venice, if you turn it on); your AI app never gets the item itself. In ChatGPT, only you see the answer; other apps get an answer written from it, which can repeat what it says. - **Secret:** passwords, recovery codes and keys. Once Olympus recognizes a Secret, it is never sent or answered from. Labels are automatic and can be wrong. Everything is stored and searched on your computer: the search index is built there, by a model small enough for a computer with 8 GB of memory. There is no hosted copy of your things, no account and no subscription. Olympus's publisher runs only a relay that passes your AI app's requests to your computer without storing them. Google sign-in happens on your computer, directly with Google. For hard private questions you can reach stronger models: [Venice](https://venice.ai) runs private models that, under Venice's own terms, keep nothing you send, and zkAPI, from OpenAnonymity and the Ethereum Foundation, hides who is asking (see [Stronger models, privately](#stronger-models-privately)). ```text you › "What did I commit to this week, across email and Telegram?" agent › Three commitments: the tax documents to Maria by Friday (email, Tue), reviewing the lease amendment (email, Mon), and the Saturday ride logistics (Telegram, Wed). [3 citations] ``` Your agent saw a bounded, cited, policy-gated answer. It never saw your mailbox. ## Get started You need a Mac with Apple silicon (M1 or later) on macOS 13 Ventura or later, or an x86_64 computer running [Omarchy](https://omarchy.org) or Ubuntu 24.04 LTS. Intel Macs, other Linux distributions and ARM Linux are not supported yet. You do not need OpenClaw, Tailscale, an API key or a new account. **1. Install Olympus on your computer.** On a Mac, open **Terminal** and run: ```bash curl -fsSL https://olympusplugin.ai/install.sh | sh ``` On Omarchy, first install the tools Olympus uses to read scans, photos and voice notes, then run the Linux installer: ```bash sudo pacman -S --needed tesseract tesseract-data-eng poppler libvips libheif ffmpeg curl -fsSL https://olympusplugin.ai/install-linux.sh | sh ``` On Ubuntu 24.04 LTS, install the prerequisites and run the Linux installer: ```bash sudo apt install curl ca-certificates tar unzip coreutils findutils gawk grep diffutils procps util-linux systemd python3 tesseract-ocr tesseract-ocr-eng poppler-utils libvips-tools libheif1 ffmpeg curl -fsSL https://olympusplugin.ai/install-linux.sh | sh ``` Each installer installs Olympus for your user only (the installer itself needs no administrator password; the package installation lines above do), checks every download against a pinned SHA-256 before using it, keeps Olympus running in the background (a LaunchAgent on a Mac, a systemd user service on Linux), adds the `olympus` command, and waits until the engine proves it is running. On Omarchy it also adds **Olympus** to the app launcher. Then Olympus downloads its built-in models once. Running it again updates or repairs the install; a failed update puts the previous version back. Details, folders and uninstall: . **2. Connect your AI.** Each app has a short guide: [ChatGPT](https://olympusplugin.ai/install/chatgpt/) · [Claude](https://olympusplugin.ai/install/claude/) · [Grok and Grok Bot](https://olympusplugin.ai/install/grok/) · [Dots](https://olympusplugin.ai/install/dots/) · [Claude Code](https://olympusplugin.ai/install/claude-code/) · [Codex](https://olympusplugin.ai/install/codex/) · [OpenClaw](https://olympusplugin.ai/install/openclaw/) · [Hermes](https://olympusplugin.ai/install/hermes/) · [any MCP app](https://olympusplugin.ai/install/other/). In ChatGPT, Claude and Grok you add Olympus's address as a connector (in ChatGPT, in Developer mode until Olympus is listed in its directory), then approve it with one click on a page Olympus opens on your own computer: there is no pairing code and no account to create. Grok Bot then uses the Grok connection. Apps on your computer, such as Claude Code, Codex and Hermes, connect with one command. **3. Connect your sources and ask.** Open the dashboard (in ChatGPT, ask *"Show my Olympus dashboard"*; on your computer, run `olympus dashboard`), connect Dropbox, Gmail or Google Drive, pick folders, and ask the way you normally would. ## Olympus for ChatGPT In ChatGPT, Olympus is a plugin. The Olympus engine runs on your computer and keeps your index there; ChatGPT asks it questions through one secure connection that you approve on that computer. ### 1. Add Olympus in ChatGPT Install Olympus on your computer first ([Get started](#get-started)). Olympus is on its way to ChatGPT's app directory. Until it is listed, add it yourself: in ChatGPT, open **Plugins**, choose **+**, then **Add custom MCP server**. Name it Olympus, choose OAuth, and paste `https://mcp.olympusplugin.ai/mcp` as the URL. If you don't see Add custom MCP server, turn on **Developer mode** in **Settings** first. OpenAI decides which accounts have Developer mode; in a work or school workspace, an admin may need to allow it. Step by step: . On Omarchy, ChatGPT may still say Olympus needs a Mac; it works on Omarchy too. ### 2. Approve ChatGPT on your computer The first time ChatGPT connects to Olympus, an Olympus page opens in your computer's browser asking *Connect ChatGPT to Olympus?* Click **Connect**. (If a page saying *Approve ChatGPT on your Mac* comes first, click **Continue on this Mac**; the page says Mac on Omarchy too.) Clicking Connect on your own computer is how Olympus knows the computer is yours: there is no code to copy and no account to create. To check on it later, run `olympus engine status` in a terminal. ### 3. Connect Dropbox and choose folders Open the **Olympus** dashboard in ChatGPT's sidebar (or ask *"Show my Olympus dashboard"*). Choose **Connect** next to Dropbox and sign in with your own Dropbox account; the sign-in link works once, for 10 minutes, from any device. Gmail and Google Drive connect the same way, except that you open their sign-in link on the computer where Olympus runs, not on a phone. Then pick folders. For each folder choose: - **Full**: Olympus reads the files and can answer from what they say. - **Names only**: Olympus keeps the file names and details such as dates, not what the files say. - **Skip**: Olympus leaves the folder alone. A folder follows its parent's choice unless you change it; **Mixed** means some folders inside it are set differently. Choose **Save and start**, and indexing begins on your computer. ### 4. Tell Olympus what's private Olympus sorts every item, one by one, into one of three tiers: - **Personal**: everyday mail, notes and files. ChatGPT can see the parts that answer your question, and cites them. - **Private**: things you keep to yourself, such as health, money or family matters. What they say is never sent to ChatGPT. Olympus answers from them on your computer, in the private answer panel (below). - **Secret**: passwords, recovery codes and keys. What Olympus recognizes as a Secret never reaches a model and is never answered from. Recognition looks for common forms (private keys, API keys, labeled passwords) and can miss others. Olympus decides on your computer. Once its built-in private model is ready, it checks every item it reads before treating it as Personal. Labels are automatic and can be wrong. In the dashboard, **Privacy** asks *"What's private for you?"*: answer in your own words. Once you do, only the kinds of things you call private are Private: health or family matters you leave out, or say are fine to share, can reach ChatGPT. You can also mark folders, Gmail labels or senders as always Private. ### 5. Ask Ask in ChatGPT the way you normally would: *"What did Sam say about the lease?"* ChatGPT searches Olympus and answers from your Personal items, with citations. Olympus also scores search matches with a built-in reranker on computers with 16 GB of memory or more (16 GiB measured RAM). Scoring runs only on this computer. Installing the search model adds one reranker download of about 136 MB; answers use the fused keyword and vector order until it is installed. The reranker is released after 10 idle minutes and loads again when needed. Set `OLYMPUS_SOURCE_RERANKER=off` to turn it off, or `built-in` to enable it on a computer with less memory. ### The private answer panel When some of the items that match your question are Private, a small Olympus panel appears on its own under ChatGPT's reply: **Private answer from your computer**, marked **Not sent to ChatGPT**. - Your computer writes the answer with its built-in private model (Qwen3.5, sized to its memory: 2B under 16 GB, 4B with more) and sends it to the panel sealed, so only the panel can open it. It goes around the ChatGPT conversation, not through it, and the Olympus relay cannot read it. - On an Apple silicon Mac it usually arrives within a minute; on Omarchy it depends on the computer's processor and can take a few minutes. Ask for *"all the details"* and Olympus reads the whole documents instead; that can take a few minutes. - **Sources** (closed at first) lists the items the answer used. Click one to open it on your computer, or in Dropbox on the web if it is not on this computer (ChatGPT opens that web link for you, so it sees the address). - **Hide** folds the answer away and **Show** brings it back. An answer expires after 10 minutes; ask again for a new one. - Ask follow-up questions in the chat as usual; each private answer appears in a new panel. Your computer needs to be awake and online. The panel runs inside ChatGPT's page, so it relies on the panel code ChatGPT loads; the [design](https://github.com/jamiezigelbaum/Olympus/blob/main/docs/design/chatgpt-plugin.md#who-can-read-the-answer) states that limit plainly. ### What ChatGPT can and can't see ChatGPT **can** see: - The parts of your Personal items that answer a question: excerpts, titles, dates and links. - File names, including the names of some Private items. A file's name can be Personal while what it says is Private, so its name may show up in ChatGPT; its contents never do. - That some items matching a question are Private: ChatGPT's model learns just that, with no titles and no content. - Status: which sources are connected, how far indexing has got, and what needs you. The folder picker shows your folder names inside ChatGPT so you can choose; they pass through ChatGPT to reach the picker, but ChatGPT's model is not given them. ChatGPT **can't** see: - What your Private items say, or the private answers made from them. - Secret items Olympus recognizes. - Folders you skip, or what the files in Names-only folders say. - API keys or passwords: you never enter one in ChatGPT. Optional extras such as a Venice account are set up on your computer. The relay at `mcp.olympusplugin.ai` passes ChatGPT's requests to your computer. It stores and logs no questions, answers or tokens, but like any HTTPS service it handles them in transit. Full details: the [ChatGPT design](https://github.com/jamiezigelbaum/Olympus/blob/main/docs/design/chatgpt-plugin.md) and the [trust model](https://github.com/jamiezigelbaum/Olympus/blob/main/docs/TRUST_MODEL.md). ## Claude, Grok and other apps Claude (web, desktop and phone) and Grok connect through the same Olympus relay as ChatGPT, with one click to approve on your computer, and Grok Bot uses the Grok connection; apps on your computer, such as Claude Code, Codex and Hermes, connect there directly. Guides: . They search what is Personal, with citations, like ChatGPT. They never get your Private items themselves or the Secrets Olympus recognizes. For Private items they get at most an answer that the private model on your computer (or Venice, if you set it up) writes from them, checked for secrets, with each item's title, path, source and author. That answer can repeat what the items say. ChatGPT is stricter: it gets no answer from Private items at all, and shows one only in its private answer panel. When an agent is not given an answer, Olympus records the question and the model built into Olympus answers it on your computer; the agent is told only that the answer is in Olympus on your computer, with a link (`olympus://open/private/` and a random identifier) that opens it there. The answer waits in the dashboard's [Inbox](https://olympusplugin.ai/open/private/) (under **On this computer**), which Olympus gives no AI app a way to read, until you delete it, and **Needs you** counts the answers you have not read. More: [Connect other agents](#connect-other-agents). ## Stronger models, privately For hard private questions you can reach stronger models without giving yourself away. Both are off until you turn them on. - **[Venice](https://venice.ai)** runs private models that, under Venice's own terms, keep nothing you send. Add your Venice key under **Keys**, on your computer. In **Ask a question**, a Venice model reads the passages of your files it needs, and is available only if your privacy settings allow Private items to go to Venice; a key alone does not allow it. - **zkAPI**, from OpenAnonymity and the Ethereum Foundation, hides who is asking. It pays anonymously and sends the question over Tor (on unless you turn it off; without Tor, your network address shows): no account, no card, no name, just proof the question is paid for. In **Strict** mode your computer first rewrites the question into general questions; **Standard**, by default, takes out names, contact details and account numbers, or sends your words as written if you choose that. What you ask can still identify you. Turn on **Anonymous answers** under **Keys** on your computer, then ask from your agent or from **Ask a question** in the dashboard's [Inbox](https://olympusplugin.ai/open/private/); each question as sent, and its reply, stay in the Inbox on your computer until you delete them or the Inbox removes the oldest when full. Anonymous answers work on a Mac and on Omarchy and Ubuntu 24.04 LTS (x64), once Olympus's network isolation checks pass. ## Uninstall On a Mac, run `curl -fsSL https://olympusplugin.ai/uninstall.sh | sh`; on Linux, `curl -fsSL https://olympusplugin.ai/uninstall-linux.sh | sh`. Both stop Olympus and remove the app, the runtime and the `olympus` command, and keep your settings and data. To delete those too, first run `olympus engine stop` and `olympus data delete --all`. To only stop Olympus and remove its login item or service, run `olympus engine uninstall`. The rest of this README covers how Olympus works and Olympus with OpenClaw, which stays supported and optional. ## How it works Olympus ingests your sources into local, trust-tiered indexes, then lets your frontier agent answer questions across all of them, with sensitive material handled only by lanes you approved: your own local models, privacy-approved private cloud inference, or not at all. Every item you ingest is judged on its own as Personal, Private, or Secrets (plus Public on installs made before 1.0; internally S0-S5): its names are Personal unless something raises them, and its content is raised to Private or Secrets on evidence. Each tier has its own index and routes only to the model lanes your sovereignty policy allows: ```mermaid flowchart LR subgraph sources["Your sources"] direction TB SRC1[Gmail · Drive · Dropbox] SRC2[Telegram · WhatsApp · X] end subgraph olympus["Olympus (local)"] direction TB ING[Ingest & classify
every item, locally] IDX[(Trust-tiered
local indexes)] POL{{Sovereignty policy
your rules, enforced}} ING --> IDX --> POL end subgraph lanes["Model lanes you approved"] direction TB CLOUD[Frontier cloud
everyday content] PRIVATE[Venice
Private content when routed] LOCAL[Your local models
Private content] end AGENT[Your agent
cited, bounded answers] sources --> ING POL --> CLOUD & PRIVATE & LOCAL CLOUD & PRIVATE & LOCAL --> AGENT ``` Olympus uses **Personal** (ordinary personal and work content), **Private** (sensitive material), and **Secrets** (once recognized, never model input). There is no Public tier on any new install, ChatGPT or OpenClaw, whichever posture you choose: anything that would have been Public is Personal. Installs made before 1.0 keep a **Public** tier. See the [tier mapping](https://github.com/jamiezigelbaum/Olympus/blob/main/docs/TRUST_MODEL.md#product-tier-names) for the unchanged storage identifiers. Four postures, chosen (and changeable) in setup — a config file, not a code fork: | Preset | Personal content | Private content: health, finance, legal, therapy, family | |---|---|---| | **Local models and private cloud** (`local-first`) | frontier cloud | approved secure pool with explicit local → [Venice](https://venice.ai) Private order | | **Local models only** (`local-only`) | frontier cloud | your own local models only | | **Private cloud only** (`private-cloud-only`) | frontier cloud | [Venice](https://venice.ai) Private model (`kimi-k3`) | | **Private meaning search on this computer** (`no-sensitive`) | frontier cloud | **stored and searched by meaning on this computer**: its search vectors come from the built-in model and are kept here; no Private agent answer lane | The engine sizes local answer prompts from the model's served context window when it can read it at startup (or the built-in model's manifest). Unknown windows keep the 13,500-byte fallback. Automatic sizing reserves answer tokens and framing space and caps prompts at 27,000 bytes, the size that kept every passage hit in measurement. `/health` lists each local answer route's `local_prompt_budget` source, so a fallback shows. `OLYMPUS_SOURCE_INDEX_LOCAL_ANALYST_PROMPT_BYTES` still overrides that size. “Private cloud only” describes **Private-data handling**: Venice answers Private questions. Search indexing for every tier uses EmbeddingGemma 2, Google's small embedding model, built into Olympus: it downloads once, runs on your computer, needs no account or key, and sends nothing anywhere. On a Mac it also reads pictures, so photos are searchable by what is in them. The embedding choices are built-in local EmbeddingGemma or Venice. Existing Gemini and local-server configurations remain compatible; see the [embedding migration guide](docs/SOVEREIGNTY_CONFIG.md#legacy-embedding-migration). Private content never goes to Gemini. Personal questions use OpenClaw's own configured default model. One question searches every tier. When it finds Private evidence, the private lane your posture approved answers it and your agent receives only the checked, cited answer. Secrets Olympus recognizes are never searched by content: it can tell you where one lives, never what it says. Some rules are not configurable, by design: secure content never routes to ordinary cloud models, recognized secrets are denied to every lane, and an exhausted policy chain refuses rather than silently downgrading. ## Get started with OpenClaw Using ChatGPT? Model-lane credentials such as Venice are privacy-mode prerequisites, not sources. Tokens live in an encrypted local secret store by default, or in an explicitly configured OS secret store when supported, never in plain text. Ingestion, classification, and indexing all run in one supervised local worker — `olympus worker install` makes it start on login. Every source syncs through the same connector-store runtime. After setup, the dashboard guides the source you choose from sign-in and scope through the first sync to cited answers, and shows the next step for a source that is blocked or degraded. You connect only the sources you want. On an existing live OpenClaw install, treat plugin install/enable, gateway restart, worker service changes, and plugin refresh as live-system changes: validate with `openclaw config validate` and `openclaw doctor --lint`, then restart only through `openclaw gateway restart` or the documented ops refresh script. The repo docs and commands should never require raw edits to OpenClaw runtime config. ## The security model Olympus is built on the assumption that the boundary *is* the product: - **Local-first ingestion.** Raw source content lands in local SQLite indexes before any model sees anything. Classification happens on your computer unless you choose Venice for it. - **Sanitized handoffs.** Agents receive answer text, excerpts of Personal items, citations, and audit counts — typed wire shapes with `raw_source_exposed: false`, re-validated client-side. Embeddings, cursors, and tokens never cross. Private items reach an agent only as answers written from them, which can repeat what they say; ChatGPT's model gets none. - **A hard membrane.** Any evidence pack containing sensitive material is barred from standard cloud lanes by two independent checks — policy validation at config load, and a runtime re-check on every request. - **Fail closed, everywhere.** No approved lane for a tier means a refusal with an honest error — never a silent fallback to a less-trusted model. - **Authenticated by default.** The worker binds loopback with bearer-token auth on every route; new installs generate the token during setup. Browser controls exchange it for a short-lived HttpOnly local session protected by same-origin and CSRF checks; the bearer is never stored by the page. - **A real exit.** `olympus data export` gives you your data; `olympus data delete --all` verifiably removes indexes, embeddings, configs, tokens, and service units. The onboarding flow, end to end: ```mermaid flowchart LR A[Install
plugin] --> B[olympus setup
pick your posture] B --> C[olympus connect
OAuth IDs · session paths · API-key stdin] C --> D[Dashboard
watch it ingest] D --> E[Ask your agent
cited answers] ``` ## Command reference | Command | What it does | |---|---| | `olympus setup --preset --yes` | writes sovereignty policy and worker auth for the chosen posture | | `olympus connect ...` | records OAuth, session, or API-key credentials with source-specific flags | | `olympus worker foreground\|install\|start\|stop\|restart\|status\|upgrade\|uninstall` | one versioned lifecycle for the local engine, foreground or supervised | | `olympus dashboard` | opens the standalone dashboard with a short-lived authorization link; no worker-token copying | | `olympus dashboard --no-open` | generates an unused opening link for an agent to hand to you | | `olympus dashboard token` | advanced compatibility access to the worker bearer; never share it in chat | | `olympus source answer "…"` | ask across your sources from the terminal | | `olympus ask "…" [--level strict\|standard]` | one question to a frontier model anonymously through zkAPI (paid from your zkAPI balance; the question only) | | `olympus archive start --path \|status\|remove --archive-id ` | asks to import an old export (such as a mail `.mbox`) or to remove an imported one; you approve on the dashboard, and `status` shows progress without any message text | | `olympus tier explain\|set\|recheck\|rules\|classifier …` | why an item has its tier, owner overrides, checking one chat's or source's privacy again, rules, and the private classifier's approval | | `olympus tier migrate plan\|approve\|run\|rollback\|purge\|status` | moves an existing install's items into per-item tiers, each step owner-approved after a dry-run plan | | `olympus doctor` | diagnoses problems, each with a fix-it hint | | `olympus data export\|delete` | your data, out — or gone | | `olympus serve` | MCP stdio server for non-OpenClaw agents | `olympus worker install` and `upgrade` atomically reconcile the generated service unit and owner-only worker environment before activation. Interrupted install or upgrade transactions recover the previous managed files when the same command is rerun. `status` reports the observed service and transaction state; it never guesses that an unreadable manager or non-regular managed path is healthy. `uninstall` removes only the supervised service and intentionally retains credentials, source configuration, and indexed data. Use the separate data lifecycle when those bytes should also be removed. Credential, scope, pairing, Disconnect, partial-sync, and source-dependency repairs do not normally require a worker restart. Follow the source card or `olympus doctor` recovery action instead. Dashboard **Disconnect** stops new scheduled and manual reads, removes the selected local account grant, and keeps indexed data and reusable developer-app registration. It does not revoke provider-side access; the card links the provider revocation page. Local data deletion remains the deliberate CLI-only flow: preview `olympus data delete --source --dry-run`, Disconnect the source, then run the command without `--dry-run`. Telegram and WhatsApp are paired sessions rather than broker grants, so their cards carry **Unpair** instead: it stops new reads and deletes this computer's pairing session, keeping indexed messages and captured media, and leaves the linked device in place at the provider for you to remove there. ### Connect other agents Open the dashboard on this computer (`olympus dashboard`). For Private items it receives only answers that Venice or a local model wrote from them, which can repeat what they say, with each item's title, path, source and author. The Agents page lists connected agents with when each was added and last used, and **Revoke** removes one. `olympus connections list|revoke|pair|add` does the same from a terminal. Each agent's steps end with a short instruction that tells it when to ask Olympus. Paste it into Claude project instructions, Grok's custom instructions or Grok Bot's skills, or load the packaged Agent Skills folder [`integrations/agent-skills/ask-olympus/`](https://github.com/jamiezigelbaum/Olympus/blob/main/integrations/agent-skills/ask-olympus/SKILL.md). ### Using Olympus from other agents (MCP) `olympus serve` exposes the same sanitized read operations — `source_answer`, `source_answer_result`, `source_index_status`, capability-gated `source_index_search`, `ask_anonymously`, `archive_import`, `privacy_item_find` and `privacy_item_set` — to any MCP-capable agent. The supported Hermes configuration narrows that server to exactly `source_answer`, `source_answer_result`, `source_index_status` and `ask_anonymously` through its per-server tool allowlist. `archive_import` (start, status, remove) lets an agent ask to import an old export the user wants searched, such as a mail `.mbox` from Google Takeout or Apple Mail. It only asks: `start` stores the path as text without opening it and returns `needs_approval`; the user approves on the Olympus dashboard on their computer (Sources, Archives), and `remove` works the same way. `status` reports each archive's progress, counts, date range and gaps, never message text. It is on the native, MCP and CLI surfaces only, not on Hermes, remote MCP or the ChatGPT relay. `privacy_item_find` and `privacy_item_set` let an agent act on "that email should be private": find the item by words from its title, sender or file name (items whose names are Private, and Secret items, are never listed), then make it Private. That is the user's decision on that one item, never a rule for its sender, chat or folder. An agent can only raise an item: making it Personal, or putting it back to the judge's label, is the user's on their own computer (`olympus tier set`). Same surfaces as `archive_import`. `ask_anonymously` sends one typed question to a frontier model through zkAPI (paid per question, anonymously, from the user's own balance; what the question says can still identify them). The first call with no `level` returns `needs_choice`: the agent asks the user once for Strict (their own model rewrites the question into general questions before it leaves) or Standard (their words, prepared as written, lightly cleaned up or by their saved instruction), then calls again with `level` and `remember: true`. Only the question goes out, never documents, and never to the provider that hosts the agent asking: a question from ChatGPT goes to Claude Sonnet by default, one from Claude Code or Claude Desktop to an OpenAI model, and a one-off `model` from the agent's own provider is refused. Setup (the zkAPI route, the writer model, the zkAPI models for questions from ChatGPT and from Claude, the spend limit) lives on the dashboard's Anonymous answers card, under Keys. Questions are asked through an agent, `olympus ask`, or **Ask a question** in the dashboard's Inbox; each question as sent, and its reply, are kept in the Inbox on your computer until you delete them or the Inbox removes the oldest when full. See [`docs/design/private-answers.md`](docs/design/private-answers.md). MCP clients cap how long one tool call may run, and an answer can take several minutes. So over MCP (local `olympus serve` and remote `/mcp` alike) and the OpenAPI tool paths, a `source_answer` that is not done by a hand-off threshold returns `{"status": "working", "job_id": …}` and keeps running. The threshold is 45 seconds for remote agents (`OLYMPUS_SOURCE_ANSWER_HANDOFF_MS`, under the MCP SDK's 60-second default request timeout) and for local `olympus serve` (`OLYMPUS_SOURCE_ANSWER_STDIO_HANDOFF_MS`, under Codex's 60-second default tool timeout); both are capped at 230000. `source_answer_result` with that `job_id` returns the answer, the same error the call would have raised, or `working` again after waiting up to a minute (never longer than the threshold). A slow `ask_anonymously` (a Tor route can take minutes) hands off the same way and is collected with the same tool. A job that runs past 20 minutes is stopped with `source_answer_deadline`, and revoking a connection drops its jobs. Remote answers share the analyst with your own assistant's answers; there is no priority lane. So the worker runs at most two remote answers at once (the analyst's lane count; `OLYMPUS_SOURCE_ANSWER_MAX_RUNNING` raises it for a multi-lane analyst) and refuses more with `source_answer_busy`, which bounds how much remote work can ever queue ahead of your own question. A caller that disconnects, or a job that reaches its deadline, stops the analyst call itself and frees the lane. A job id is readable only by the connection (or `olympus serve` process) that asked, lives in memory, and expires 15 minutes after its answer is ready. For Hermes Agent, resolve the installed plugin first: ```bash openclaw plugins inspect olympus --json ``` Copy `plugin.rootDir` from that content-free response, append `/bin/olympus`, and pass the resulting absolute executable path to Hermes: ```bash hermes mcp add olympus --command /absolute/managed/olympus/bin/olympus --args serve hermes mcp test olympus ``` Make the `olympus` server entry in `~/.hermes/config.yaml` match the packaged [`config/hermes/olympus.mcp.yaml`](config/hermes/olympus.mcp.yaml): ```yaml mcp_servers: olympus: command: /bin/olympus args: [serve] tools: include: [source_answer, source_answer_result, source_index_status, ask_anonymously] prompts: false resources: false ``` Restart Hermes or run `/reload-mcp`, then verify that the discovered registered names are exactly `mcp_olympus_source_answer`, `mcp_olympus_source_answer_result`, `mcp_olympus_source_index_status` and `mcp_olympus_ask_anonymously`. Invoke the discovered names rather than hard-coding them. A cited-answer round trip uses the discovered `mcp_olympus_source_answer`; `source_watch_*` remains OpenClaw-only. The optional packaged Hermes skill is [`integrations/hermes/ask-sources/SKILL.md`](integrations/hermes/ask-sources/SKILL.md). It is also published on ClawHub, which Hermes's skills hub searches, so `hermes skills install clawhub/olympus-hermes` installs it. Or copy its directory to `~/.hermes/skills/ask-sources/` or expose the parent with `skills.external_dirs`; it declares the same four tools and no fallback access. No `hermes://mcp/install` link is published: current Hermes upstream documents custom MCP installation through `hermes mcp add` but does not document that URI handler. There are no operator agent tools. Index maintenance — sync, extraction, embedding, retries — is the worker's own scheduler, and what a person drives by hand goes through the `olympus` CLI. The whole agent tool surface is sixteen tools — `argus_ping`, `argus_list_models`, `argus_complete`, `source_answer`, `source_answer_result` (MCP and remote only), `source_index_status`, `source_index_search`, `source_watch_create`, `source_watches`, `source_watch_cancel`, `olympus_doctor`, `olympus_setup_status`, `ask_anonymously`, `archive_import`, `privacy_item_find`, `privacy_item_set` — declared in [`src/core/public-surface.ts`](src/core/public-surface.ts); Hermes over MCP sees the subset above, and worker bearer auth is enforced throughout. Operational note for connector-store corpora: a source with an account folder (Gmail, Drive, Dropbox, local files, Readwise, X, Telegram, WhatsApp, imported archives) keeps its stores where Olympus places them, and its `OLYMPUS_SOURCE_INDEX_CONNECTOR_STORES_JSON` entry names no path: it only adds a principal to the store its lane opened. A store only the mount list places (Reflect, Roam) is mounted with the same corpus id, `family`, `trustDomain` and `dbPath` its sync script writes, and that corpus id must be in the corpus registry — a store mounted for an unregistered corpus fills but is never read. Chat-family mounts must also declare their exact principal identity with `principalProvider` and `principalAccountScope` (for example, `whatsapp` and `personal`). Structured scopes use the stored account scope as their prefix, so the shipped WhatsApp identity is `personal:chat:` while Telegram remains `telegram.personal:chat:`. A chat mount without both fields remains available for non-`chat_scope` reads, but `chat_scope` filtering fails closed as not configured; mounted rows never establish account authority. The migration-era indexes, replay/import utilities, read-authority switches, and retired store writers were removed in Slice 2. Canonical connector stores are now the only source read/write authority. Compatibility aliases that remain at input boundaries do not select another runtime or store. ## Development Olympus is TypeScript on Bun: one plugin package, stable versioned architecture contracts (`SourceConnector` / `EvidencePack` / `Analyst` — only the connector is per-source), and 3,400+ tests including an architecture guard that keeps per-source answer logic out of the shared spine. ```bash bun install bun run test:focus -- test/example.test.ts ``` Use focused local proof while editing; GitHub requires each substantive CI lane and runs the complete suite in parallel before merge. See the canonical [engineering process](https://github.com/jamiezigelbaum/Olympus/blob/main/docs/ENGINEERING_PROCESS.md). Deep-dive docs: [contracts and architecture](https://github.com/jamiezigelbaum/Olympus/blob/main/docs/CONTRACTS.md) · [trust model](https://github.com/jamiezigelbaum/Olympus/blob/main/docs/TRUST_MODEL.md) · [sovereignty config](https://github.com/jamiezigelbaum/Olympus/blob/main/docs/SOVEREIGNTY_CONFIG.md) · [uninstall](https://github.com/jamiezigelbaum/Olympus/blob/main/docs/UNINSTALL.md) ## License [MIT](https://github.com/jamiezigelbaum/Olympus/blob/main/LICENSE) — free for any use, including commercial. Olympus is provided as is, without warranty; keep your own backups. Olympus is published by Open Coordination Unlimited, Inc. Its hosted relay is governed by the [Terms of Service](https://olympusplugin.ai/terms/) and [Privacy Policy](https://olympusplugin.ai/privacy/). Third-party data notices: [docs/THIRD_PARTY_DATA.md](docs/THIRD_PARTY_DATA.md). Want to suggest a change? See [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md): fork, branch, open a PR. Read access doesn't include direct pushes — everything lands through review.

repository.readme:
EN | 简 | 繁 | KO | JA | PT

Token Monitor

One live dashboard for every AI coding tool, synced across every machine.

## What is Token Monitor? A desktop app that shows live token usage and AI Tool Limits across 54+ AI coding tools — Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, GitHub Copilot, Cherry Studio, and more — with real-time multi-device sync, historical usage trends, and breakdowns by tool, device, model, session, or project. It lives wherever you look: the main window, the MacBook notch, the menu bar or system tray, the edge of the screen, a floating bubble, and native macOS widgets. ## Supported Tools Token usage, AI Tool Limits and session details from the AI coding tools and providers you already use:

See what each tool supports and where its data is read from →

## Showcase ### On your desktop

Notch Panel — running sessions beside the notch; swipe down for today's usage, every account's limits, sessions and breakdowns

Edge Dock — quotas and usage parked at the screen edge; hover for limits, recent sessions and tokens
Menu bar & tray — pick a preset or compose your own: tool icons, quota bars, reset times, cost or live tok/s
### Inside the app

Multiple accounts side by side, one-click switch of the active Codex account
Click any tool to expand input / output and cache-hit detail
Open a single session to break each prompt into tokens and tools used
More views — projects, models and devices

Usage and cost per project, aggregated across tools and devices
Every model's usage and cost, aggregated across tools
Each device's usage, cost, and sync status — expand for per-machine detail
### Usage Dashboard

A year of activity heatmap and streaks, aggregated across all devices
A year of daily trends, stacked by tool / model, with K-line
## Why Token Monitor? Most usage monitors are useful on the machine they run on. Token Monitor is built for multi-device work: each device watches its own local logs, sends summary updates to your hub, and every connected widget sees token changes almost immediately. ## Quick Install On macOS, install through the official [Homebrew Cask](https://formulae.brew.sh/cask/token-monitor): ```bash brew install --cask token-monitor ``` Or download the app for macOS, Windows, or Linux from [GitHub Releases](https://github.com/Javis603/token-monitor/releases). Launch the app to start tracking this device locally, with no hub setup required. See [Installation](#installation) for full details. ## Features ### Tracking usage - **Live token tracking** — Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, GitHub Copilot, Antigravity, OpenCode, and 42+ AI tools, with the UI updating within seconds of each turn (full list in the table above) - **Live token rate** — an optional live readout of generation speed in `tok/s` or total burn in `tok/min` - **Per-session detail** — open a session to see tokens per prompt, expandable to each reply's exact token split and tools used (read on-demand from local transcripts or databases, never synced) - **Cache hit statistics** — click any tool or model to expand a detailed breakdown of input tokens (cache hit vs miss), output tokens, and hit-rate percentages - **Cost & currency** — cost alongside token counts, shown in USD, CNY, TWD, HKD, KRW, JPY, BRL and other supported currencies; exchange rates auto-update daily and can be manually overridden in Settings - **Custom scan paths** — point a tool at extra session folders when yours live outside the defaults - **WSL usage (Windows)** — file-based usage from running WSL distros is merged about every 5 minutes; SQLite-backed tools such as OpenCode and Hermes may require a [headless agent inside WSL](docs/wsl-sqlite-setup.md) ### Limits, trends & export - **AI Tool Limits detection** — provider-specific session, daily, weekly, billing, and credits windows for Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, OpenRouter, third-party APIs, GLM, Kimi, and 34+ providers, including multiple OpenRouter/third-party profiles and balance-style accounts (Claude credits, DeepSeek prepaid balance and spend history, third-party balances) - **Multiple accounts & Codex switching** — track several accounts per provider, each with its own limits; a tracked Codex account can be switched as the active local account in one click, without re-authenticating - **Codex reset forecast** — an optional third-party forecast below Codex limits, showing the expected reset time, the reset type (Regular or Banked), and when the window last reset - **Preserve deleted session usage** — many tools prune old sessions (Claude Code drops transcripts after 30 days by default), losing that history. When enabled, Token Monitor archives observed daily tool/model usage locally so the heatmap and trends survive even after the source files are gone (see [Session data retention](#session-data-retention) below) - **Usage Trends & Dashboard** — a home-screen activity heatmap and trend chart, plus a dedicated dashboard window with streaks and stacked per-tool/per-model history (bar and K-line views) across all your devices - **Fixed usage ranges** — switch between This week, Last 7 days, and Last 30 days alongside the native day, month, and total periods - **Optional Status view** — official provider status pages, with manual or interval re-checks - **Data export** — export usage as tool-agnostic CSV + JSON, manually or auto-written to a folder, for spreadsheets, Obsidian, Grafana, or scripts; see [docs/export.md](docs/export.md) - **Subscription records** — record by hand what each AI account actually costs; the plan label's tooltip then reports the price, the next renewal or end date, time subscribed, and the month's usage cost as a multiple of what the plan costs, for recurring plans and top-up ledgers alike ### Multi-device & deployment - **Real-time multi-device sync** — hub-backed sync uses Server-Sent Events to push updates to other devices within seconds; iCloud Drive sync is eventually consistent - **Local-first** — no servers needed for single-device use - **Self-hosted sync backend** — in-widget hub, Node CLI hub, or Cloudflare Worker - **Headless agent** — reports usage from servers, SSH hosts, and WSL without the desktop app; see [Headless agent](#headless-agent) - **iOS widget support** — Widgy and Scriptable through the Worker hub - **Privacy-first** — prompts, responses, source code, and file contents stay on your machine ### Interface & surfaces - **Notch Panel (macOS)** — running and waiting sessions sit beside the notch (or in a pill on screens without one); hover or swipe down to open pages for today's usage and the last seven days, every account's limits side by side, active and recent sessions, and tool / model breakdowns - **Edge Dock (macOS & Windows)** — keeps quotas and usage at the screen edge, with auto-hide, always-visible, or fullscreen auto-hide modes. Hover cards show account limits, recent sessions, and token usage. Choose, reorder, and configure items in Settings, and toggle it from the menu bar or system tray - **Menu bar (macOS) and system tray (Windows) popover** — live cost, tokens, or the closest-to-empty provider limit % next to the icon - **Menu bar layout composer** — the menu bar and the floating bubble can use a built-in preset or a layout you build yourself: pick "Custom…" to add AI tool icons, quota bars, percentages, reset times, cost, the live token rate, or custom text, drag to reorder against a live preview, and give each item its own AI tool, account, quota window, and typeface - **Floating Bubble mode** — collapses the widget into a draggable mini-window with click or hover preview and tray-style content - **Native macOS Widgets** — View token usage and cost, trends, AI tool quota remaining and reset times, activity heatmaps, and breakdowns by tool or model in Small, Medium, and Large layouts on macOS 14+ - **Breakdown views** — grouped by tool, device, model, session, project, or account limits - **Appearance controls** — interface theme switching (incl. a light mode), per-tool vendor colours, glass opacity, blur, transparent window mode, and custom fonts - **Customizable tool list** — hide, pin, and reorder tools in the main dashboard without changing what gets tracked - **Recordable global shortcut** — show or hide the window from anywhere - **Discord Rich Presence** — broadcast today's tokens, cost, and top client (opt-in) ### Plugins (experimental) Extend desktop pages with custom content, add plugin pages and settings, and place content in Notch, Edge Dock, the menu bar/system tray or floating bubbles. Authors can build their own interfaces and optional local Node backends for data sources and computation. Manage plugins in Settings → Plugins. See the [user guide](https://javis-ai.com/token-monitor/docs/plugins.html?lang=en), [community plugins](https://github.com/Javis603/token-monitor-plugins), [development guide](docs/plugins/author-quickstart.md) and [Plugin API](docs/plugins/README.md). The plugin API is experimental and may change; plugins may need updates. Enable only code you trust: plugins are not sandboxed, and Node backends run with your OS user’s permissions. ## Supported Tools in Detail Token Monitor supports token usage, account-limit checks, and Notes, Custom balance endpoints, and data paths overridden by environment variables
- Paths above are the defaults. Token Monitor follows the same environment overrides Tokscale does — `$XDG_DATA_HOME` for the `~/.local/share/` roots, and per-tool variables such as `$CODEX_HOME`, `$GEMINI_CLI_HOME`, `$SENPI_CODING_AGENT_DIR`, `$SENPI_CODING_AGENT_SESSION_DIR`, `$GROK_HOME`, `$HERMES_HOME`, `$GOOSE_PATH_ROOT`, `$KIMI_CODE_HOME`, `$UNSLOTH_STUDIO_HOME`, `$LM_STUDIO_HOME`, `$DSH_HOME`, `$REASONIX_STATE_HOME`, `$REASONIX_HOME` and the `$CLINE_*` family. - Gemini CLI supports `$GEMINI_CLI_HOME` on the host; WSL discovery checks only the default Linux `~/.gemini/tmp/`. Fresh installs track it by default; existing saved tool selections must enable it in Settings → tools. - Muse Code subscription limits use `muse usage --json` from Muse Code 1.4.13+ and its existing sign-in. Missing allowance and API-key billing do not provide quota percentages. See the [Muse data-source notes](docs/providers/muse.md). - Goose counts all session usage on its creation day, including usage on later days. Remote goosed servers and custom scan paths are not supported. See [Goose source notes](docs/providers/goose.md). - CatPaw is off by default; enable it in Settings → tools. It reads domestic and overseas assistant databases on macOS and Windows. See [CatPaw source notes](docs/providers/catpaw.md) for paths and verification boundaries. - OmO Native tracks local session records from both OmO Native and standalone Senpi. A fresh install tracks it. An existing saved Tools selection does not gain it on upgrade; enable OmO Native in Settings → tools. Some child-task logs count toward usage but do not yet support Session Detail. See [OmO Native source notes](docs/providers/senpi.md). - LM Studio tracking currently covers OpenAI-compatible `/v1/chat/completions` and `/v1/responses` requests recorded in server logs. Conversations started from LM Studio's built-in Chat UI and native `/api/v1/chat` requests are not included. - Unsloth Studio tracks inference usage from `studio.db`: Studio chats and its local API. Local inference has zero API cost; recognized metered providers use Tokscale's price estimates. Training tokens are not included. See [Unsloth source notes](docs/providers/unsloth.md). - Devin tracks Devin CLI sessions from the local `sessions.db` and Devin Desktop agent sessions from `acp-events` ACP logs; where both cover the same session the CLI database is authoritative. Desktop coverage depends on the connected ACP agent: only agents that write `usage_update` events locally are counted, and Devin Desktop's default `devin-cloud` agent meters its usage server-side, so a default Desktop setup reports no Desktop tokens. Session titles and project attribution come from the CLI database. See [Devin source notes](docs/providers/devin.md). - Notion AI uses internal APIs with a manually pasted `token_v2` cookie and an explicit Business/Enterprise workspace ID. Only fixtures have been validated; a real response sample is unavailable and live authentication awaits approval. There is no automatic cookie retrieval or public API guarantee. See [Notion source notes](docs/providers/notion.md). - Manus reads a signed-in desktop session on macOS/Windows, or a manually supplied web session on any OS (including Linux). Monthly credits, refresh allowance and balance use the same undocumented internal endpoint, with no compatibility guarantee. See [Manus source notes](docs/providers/manus.md). - Hark reads the signed-in macOS desktop session, or a pasted session cookie on any OS. It shows account-level daily and monthly token pools. See [Hark source notes](docs/providers/hark.md). - MiniMax Code reads the local session history the CLI writes, under `~/.minimax` or `MINIMAX_DATA_DIR` / `MAVIS_DATA_DIR` (also `~/.mavis` and `~/.minimax-` / `~/.mavis-`), plus runs captured with `tokscale headless mcode`; a turn found in both counts once. - Command Code transcripts do not contain actual token counts or per-message model metadata. Token usage is estimated from transcript text, while model attribution and derived cost may reflect the currently configured model rather than the model historically used for each request. - The Cursor cache comes from Cursor's account-level usage export, so it covers usage from Cursor IDE, Cursor CLI, and Grok Bot. Token Monitor automatically detects accounts signed in through the Cursor desktop app and also supports adding accounts manually in Settings. The cache re-syncs automatically when stale, but newly finished sessions can take a few minutes to reach Cursor's dashboard, so recent usage may still appear with a delay. - Custom maps numeric JSON fields from one GET balance endpoint; OpenAI or Anthropic compatibility alone is not enough. - Qoder: the Qoder group in Settings → tools tracks the international and CN editions independently. Fresh installations track both; existing selections are preserved. The tool usage list combines them unless **Show versions separately** is on. International transcripts are read from `QODER_CONFIG_DIR/projects` (default `~/.qoder/projects`); CN transcripts from `TOKEN_MONITOR_QODER_CN_PROJECTS_PATH`, then `QODERCN_CONFIG_DIR/projects` (default `~/.qoder-cn/projects`). Only token counts recorded in transcripts are counted: managed-model rows that record credits without tokens are left out, and those credits stay in AI Tool Limits. Qoder CN CLI 1.1.62 has been reported to record future counters with `QODERCN_EXPOSE_TOKEN_USAGE=1`; existing records are not backfilled. Dynamic model slots such as `dfmodel` are shown as recorded. Older Qoder CN releases that stored usage only in SQLite are no longer collected; existing Token Monitor history files are kept. See [Qoder source notes](docs/providers/qodercn.md).
### Additional Feature Support | Feature | Supported tools/sources | Notes | |---------|-------------------------|------------| | Session titles | Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Cursor, Antigravity, Cline CLI, Factory Droid, Kimi CLI, Grok Build, Pi, Oh My Pi, OmO Native, MiMo, ZCode, CodeBuddy, WorkBuddy, Reasonix, DeepSeek Harness, Cherry Studio, Devin CLI, fx, MiniMax Code | — | | Per-prompt/reply usage and tool calls | Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Pi, Oh My Pi, OmO Native, CodeBuddy, WorkBuddy, Reasonix, DeepSeek Harness | Details are read locally and are not synced. | | Context usage/remaining space | Claude Code, Codex, DeepSeek Harness | Claude Code's context limit is estimated from the model. | | Cache usage/session cache hit rate | Sources exposing cache fields, including Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Cursor, Kimi, Pi, Oh My Pi, OmO Native, DeepSeek Harness | Hit rate is shown when cache usage data is available. | | Estimated cache time remaining | Claude Code | 5 minutes or 1 hour, based on the recorded cache tier. | | Output speed/token consumption rate | Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Antigravity, Kimi, GitHub Copilot, Pi, Oh My Pi, OmO Native, Kilo CLI, MiMo Code/MiMo Desktop, Muse Code, ZCode CLI, Kiro, DeepSeek Harness, Devin CLI | Output speed in `tok/s`, total token consumption in `tok/min`; timing can include waiting. | | Session model and reasoning effort | Claude Code, Codex | Only models and reasoning effort explicitly recorded in the session are shown. | | Reasoning token counts | Codex, OpenCode, Pi, Oh My Pi, OmO Native, CodeBuddy, WorkBuddy, Reasonix, DeepSeek Harness | — | | Turn start/completion detection | Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Cursor, CodeBuddy, WorkBuddy, DeepSeek Harness | Uses turn signals recorded by the tool. For other tools or without valid signals, running is estimated for about 10 minutes after the last activity. | | Native running/waiting-for-input status | Claude Code, Codex | — | | Parent/subagent grouping | Codex, Antigravity, Oh My Pi, ZCode; T3 Code sessions with verifiable parent links | Claude Code grouping is available through T3 Code. | | Continuation-record grouping for the same conversation | Codex; T3 Code sessions with verified thread links | — | | Switch local accounts | Codex | Switches between accounts added in Token Monitor. | | Quota reset times/countdowns | Sources exposing reset times, e.g. Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Cursor, Antigravity | — | | Available quota reset credits/grants | Claude Code, Codex | Shows remaining resets and expiry dates; display only. | | Quota reset forecast | Codex | Optional third-party forecasts from codex-resets.com. | ## Installation On macOS, install through the official [Homebrew Cask](https://formulae.brew.sh/cask/token-monitor): ```bash brew install --cask token-monitor ``` Or download from [GitHub Releases](https://github.com/Javis603/token-monitor/releases). - **macOS (Apple Silicon)** — `.dmg`, signed and notarized - **macOS (Intel)** — x64 `.dmg`, signed and notarized - **Windows 10/11** — setup and portable `.exe`, [code-signed](docs/code-signing.md) - **Linux x64** — `.AppImage` Packaged builds check GitHub Releases automatically. When an update is available, the app shows an update indicator; supported platforms can also install from Settings → General. ### First run Local mode is the default: launch the app and it starts tracking this device. No hub, agent, or config required. ## Multi-device sync Pick ONE multi-device sync backend for your devices (and any headless agents). On each device, open the widget and pick a mode under Settings → Multi-device Sync. The widget contributes this device's usage automatically; run the [headless agent](#headless-agent) only on machines without a widget. iCloud Drive is a macOS-widget-only option and does not support headless agents. #### Option A — Host the hub from the widget (easiest, no CLI) In the widget on one always-on machine, open Settings → Multi-device Sync and pick **Host hub on this device**. The widget generates a random secret and lists the LAN URLs other devices can connect to (Tailscale or ZeroTier addresses appear here too). On every other device, pick **Connect to a hub** and paste the URL + secret. The hub runs while Token Monitor is running — quitting (not just closing the window) stops it for all connected devices. #### Option B — Self-hosted Node hub (always-on headless machine) ```bash # on the always-on machine cp .env.example .env # set TOKEN_MONITOR_SECRET to something private, then: npm run hub ``` #### Option C — Cloudflare Worker hub (across networks, including iPhone) [![Deploy to Cloudflare](https://deploy.workers.cloudflare.com/button)](https://deploy.workers.cloudflare.com/?url=https://github.com/Javis603/token-monitor/tree/main/worker) One-click deploy — Cloudflare will prompt for the `TOKEN_MONITOR_SECRET` during setup. Or deploy manually: ```bash cd worker npm install npx wrangler login npx wrangler secret put TOKEN_MONITOR_SECRET npx wrangler deploy ``` Paste the deployed URL into each device's widget at Settings → Multi-device Sync. See [worker/README.md](worker/README.md) for the iOS widget recipe and endpoint reference, or [docs/API.md](docs/API.md) for the hub HTTP API. #### Option D — iCloud Drive (macOS, no Hub server) On each Mac signed into the same Apple ID, choose **iCloud Drive** in Settings → Multi-device Sync. This is an opt-in macOS-only path: Token Monitor writes one atomic snapshot per device and one subscription snapshot per writer under `iCloud Drive/Token Monitor/sync-v1/`, then each Mac aggregates the valid files locally. It uses no Token Monitor server, CloudKit, or credentials; provider API keys, cookies, and tokens stay local. iCloud Drive is eventually consistent, so another Mac may take a moment to appear or update, and a missing or malformed file never clears the last-good aggregate. ### Headless agent Run the headless agent on servers, SSH hosts, or inside WSL — anywhere you use AI tools without the desktop widget. It collects usage on that machine and posts it to your hub (Option A, B, or C). Requires Node.js 22.15+ and git. ```bash git clone https://github.com/Javis603/token-monitor.git cd token-monitor npm ci cp .env.example .env # set TOKEN_MONITOR_HUB_URL, TOKEN_MONITOR_SECRET, and a unique TOKEN_MONITOR_DEVICE_ID npm run agent # run continuously ``` See [docs/headless-agent.md](docs/headless-agent.md) for running it as a service, updating, uninstalling, and troubleshooting. For SQLite-backed tools inside WSL, follow the [WSL SQLite setup](docs/wsl-sqlite-setup.md). ## App data App state lives in the OS user-data dir — delete it along with the app to fully uninstall. | Platform | Path | |----------|------| | macOS | `~/Library/Application Support/Token Monitor/` | | Windows | `%APPDATA%/Token Monitor/` | | Linux | `~/.config/Token Monitor/` | ## Build from source To build your own installer, use Node.js 22.15+ on the **target** OS (electron-builder can't cross-build a macOS `.dmg` on Windows, or vice-versa). ```bash npm install npm run dist:mac # macOS arm64 .dmg → dist/ npm run dist:mac:x64 # macOS Intel x64 .dmg → dist/ npm run dist:win # Windows x64 installer .exe → dist/ npm run dist:linux # Linux x64 AppImage → dist/ npm run pack # unpacked app dir (no installer), for quick local testing ``` Output lands in `dist/`. Windows and Linux use the matching `dist:*` script above on the target OS. Packaging the macOS release build requires a local Developer ID Application signing identity; use `npm start` for local development or unsupported platforms. Runtime and packaging scripts explicitly ensure the pinned tokscale binary on every target with a vendored build. Other source platforms keep the npm binary and filter clients it does not support; `npm install`, lint, and tests do not download it. For lint and tests, run `npm run verify`. Run `npm run test:coverage` for JavaScript coverage reports; see [testing and coverage](docs/testing.md) for scope, report files and interpretation limits. ## How it works ```text Mode A — Local (default, no setup) widget (Electron) ──▶ tokscale ──▶ ~/.claude, ~/.codex, $HERMES_HOME Mode B — Sync (opt-in, multi-device) device A widget ──▶ device B widget ──▶ hub ──▶ widget on any device device C agent ──▶ ``` The widget chooses local vs sync mode based on Settings → Multi-device Sync. The hub itself can run as a separate `npm run hub` process, a Cloudflare Worker, or directly inside one of the widgets (Host mode). In Hub Client and Host modes, the hub pushes aggregated stats to every connected widget over Server-Sent Events, so updates on one device usually appear on the others within a few seconds. iCloud Drive mode syncs files directly; propagation is eventually consistent and may take longer. ## Session data retention With **Preserve deleted session usage** enabled (Settings → Collection), Token Monitor archives observed daily tool/model usage locally with no time limit — so even after a source tool prunes its own sessions, the heatmap and trends are unaffected.
Advanced: extend the source tool's own retention
The heatmap and sync payload use a rolling 370-day window (older observations remain available locally for future views). **Claude Code keeps only 30 days of transcripts by default** (`cleanupPeriodDays`); to keep the full rolling year before the archive kicks in, raise it in `~/.claude/settings.json` before the window passes: ```json { "cleanupPeriodDays": 370 } ``` A larger value keeps more, at the cost of transcripts living on disk for as long as you set. tokscale's [Session Data Retention](https://github.com/junhoyeo/tokscale#session-data-retention) table covers the other tools' defaults and config paths. This archive only covers days Token Monitor has already observed; data deleted before it started tracking cannot be recovered.
## Settings There are two places to configure Token Monitor; day-to-day use only needs the first: - **Widget (GUI)** — click the `⚙` button in the bottom-right corner. Sections, in order: General (language, launch at login, updates), Main (Home modules and display currency), Window (window behavior, menu bar and floating-bubble layout, tray mode, shortcut), Appearance (theme and vendor colours), Collection (tracked tools, collection cadence, Preserve deleted session usage, data export), AI Tool Limits (provider selection, limits, and credentials), Subscriptions (what you pay per account), and Multi-device Sync. The `⇧` button in the title bar cycles the window behavior. - **Headless agent & hub** — no UI; configured with a `.env` file at the project root (copy from `.env.example`), precedence CLI flag → env var → built-in default. See [docs/configuration.md](docs/configuration.md#headless-agent--hub-env). See the [configuration reference](docs/configuration.md) for every setting and all environment variables. ## Privacy Token Monitor processes usage logs locally and sends no analytics or telemetry to the project maintainer. Network access occurs only for documented or user-enabled features. See the [privacy policy](docs/privacy.md) for the data used by updates, provider integrations, Discord Rich Presence, and optional multi-device sync. ## Star History ## Contributing Issues and PRs are welcome. Start with [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md); project conventions, architecture notes, and the command reference live in [AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md). ## Acknowledgments - [tokscale](https://github.com/junhoyeo/tokscale) for log parsing and token accounting. - [CodexBar](https://github.com/steipete/CodexBar) for AI Tool Limits research. - [Code signing policy](docs/code-signing.md): Free code signing provided by [SignPath.io](https://signpath.io/), certificate by [SignPath Foundation](https://signpath.org/). ## License [MIT](LICENSE) © [@Javis](https://github.com/Javis603)

name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:

permissions:
  contents: read

concurrency:
  group: ci-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: true

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ${{ matrix.os }}
    # Bound stalled test runs instead of waiting for GitHub's six-hour default.
    timeout-minutes: 15
    strategy:
      fail-fast: false
      matrix:
        # Both supported Node versions on Linux; latest-Node smoke on macOS/Windows to
        # catch platform-specific bugs (tray on macOS, WSL/paths on Windows).
        os: [ubuntu-latest]
        node-version: ['22', '24']
        include:
          - os: macos-latest
            node-version: '24'
          - os: windows-latest
            node-version: '24'
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: ${{ matrix.node-version }}
          cache: npm
      - run: npm ci
      - name: Verify vendored worker shared code is in sync
        # Drift check is OS-independent; running it once on Linux avoids
        # false positives from Windows CRLF checkout vs the LF sync writes.
        if: runner.os == 'Linux'
        run: |
          npm run sync:worker
          git diff --exit-code worker/src/shared \
            || { echo "::error::worker/src/shared is stale — run 'npm run sync:worker' and commit."; exit 1; }
      - run: npm run lint
      - name: Run tests with coverage
        id: coverage
        if: runner.os == 'Linux' && matrix.node-version == '24'
        run: npm run test:coverage
      - name: Run tests
        if: runner.os != 'Linux' || matrix.node-version != '24'
        run: npm test
      - name: Upload coverage reports
        if: ${{ !cancelled() && (steps.coverage.outcome == 'success' || steps.coverage.outcome == 'failure') }}
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@043fb46d1a93c77aae656e7c1c64a875d1fc6a0a # v7.0.1
        with:
          name: javascript-coverage
          path: |
            coverage/
            !coverage/tmp/**
          if-no-files-found: error
          retention-days: 14

  timezones:
    # Every GitHub-hosted runner sets its clock to UTC on every OS, so the
    # os × node matrix above varies two axes and still samples a single UTC
    # offset. Usage periods are cut at *local* midnight, so an assertion written
    # against a UTC instant is green there by construction and the first person
    # to see it red is a contributor running `npm run verify` at home.
    #
    # This is a list rather than "UTC plus one other" because each offset failed
    # a different subset of the suite (#481): +02 and +10 were green while +07
    # was not, and Kathmandu is here because +05:45 is not a whole hour.
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    # Allow for seven sequential suite runs while still bounding stalls.
    timeout-minutes: 30
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: '24'
          cache: npm
      - run: npm ci
      - name: Run the suite at several UTC offsets
        # Overlap I/O and real timer waits inside each suite without adding
        # runners or running multiple timezone suites simultaneously.
        run: |
          for tz in Asia/Ho_Chi_Minh Asia/Kathmandu Pacific/Chatham America/Los_Angeles Pacific/Honolulu Pacific/Pago_Pago Pacific/Kiritimati; do
            echo "::group::TZ=$tz"
            TZ="$tz" node --test --test-concurrency=8 "tests/**/*.test.js"
            echo "::endgroup::"
          done

  mac-widget:
    runs-on: macos-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: '24'
          cache: npm
      - run: npm ci
      - name: Run macOS Widget Node tests
        run: >-
          node --test
          tests/shared/macWidgetSnapshot.test.js
          tests/electron/macWidgetBridge.test.js
          tests/electron/macWidgetDeepLink.test.js
          tests/electron/macWidgetHistory.test.js
          tests/electron/macWidgetHistoryStore.test.js
          tests/electron/macWidgetSnapshotController.test.js
          tests/electron/macWidgetSnapshotLane.test.js
          tests/electron/macWidgetLaunchServicesRecovery.test.js
          tests/electron/macWidgetReloader.test.js
          tests/electron/macWidgetSigning.test.js
          tests/electron/macosProvisioning.test.js
          tests/electron/macWidgetIntegration.test.js
          tests/electron/macWidgetVerifier.test.js
      - name: Run native macOS Widget tests
        run: >-
          xcodebuild
          -project native/macos/TokenMonitorWidget.xcodeproj
          -scheme TokenMonitorWidget
          -destination 'platform=macOS'
          test
          CODE_SIGNING_ALLOWED=NO
      - name: Build and verify arm64 Widget extension
        env:
          TOKEN_MONITOR_WIDGET_ARCH: arm64
        run: |
          npm run build:mac-widget
          test -d build/macos-widget/TokenMonitorWidget.appex
          test -x build/macos-widget/TokenMonitorWidgetReloader
          test "$(lipo -archs build/macos-widget/TokenMonitorWidget.appex/Contents/MacOS/TokenMonitorWidget)" = "arm64"
          test "$(lipo -archs build/macos-widget/TokenMonitorWidgetReloader)" = "arm64"
          test "$(/usr/libexec/PlistBuddy -c 'Print :com.apple.security.application-groups:0' build/macos-widget/TokenMonitorWidget.entitlements)" = "group.com.example.tokenmonitor"
      - name: Package and verify a complete local Widget app
        env:
          TOKEN_MONITOR_WIDGET_ENABLED: '1'
          TOKEN_MONITOR_WIDGET_ARCH: arm64
          TOKEN_MONITOR_APP_GROUP: group.com.example.tokenmonitor
          TOKEN_MONITOR_WIDGET_BUNDLE_ID: com.example.tokenmonitor.widget
          TOKEN_MONITOR_LOCAL_DEVELOPMENT_SIGNING: '1'
          CSC_FOR_PULL_REQUEST: 'true'
        run: |
          npm run pack:mac:widget
          npm run verify:mac:widget-app
      - name: Build and verify x64 Widget extension
        env:
          TOKEN_MONITOR_WIDGET_ARCH: x64
        run: |
          npm run build:mac-widget
          test -d build/macos-widget/TokenMonitorWidget.appex
          test -x build/macos-widget/TokenMonitorWidgetReloader
          test "$(lipo -archs build/macos-widget/TokenMonitorWidget.appex/Contents/MacOS/TokenMonitorWidget)" = "x86_64"
          test "$(lipo -archs build/macos-widget/TokenMonitorWidgetReloader)" = "x86_64"
          test "$(/usr/libexec/PlistBuddy -c 'Print :com.apple.security.application-groups:0' build/macos-widget/TokenMonitorWidget.entitlements)" = "group.com.example.tokenmonitor"
      - name: Package and verify a complete x64 local Widget app
        env:
          TOKEN_MONITOR_WIDGET_ENABLED: '1'
          TOKEN_MONITOR_WIDGET_ARCH: x64
          TOKEN_MONITOR_APP_GROUP: group.com.example.tokenmonitor
          TOKEN_MONITOR_WIDGET_BUNDLE_ID: com.example.tokenmonitor.widget
          TOKEN_MONITOR_LOCAL_DEVELOPMENT_SIGNING: '1'
          CSC_FOR_PULL_REQUEST: 'true'
        run: |
          npm run pack:mac:widget:x64
          npm run verify:mac:widget-app -- "dist/mac-x64/mac/Token Monitor.app"
      - name: Check Widget CI diff
        run: git diff --check

EN | 简 | 繁 | KO | JA | PT

Token Monitor

One live dashboard for every AI coding tool, synced across every machine.

## What is Token Monitor? A desktop app that shows live token usage and AI Tool Limits across 54+ AI coding tools — Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, GitHub Copilot, Cherry Studio, and more — with real-time multi-device sync, historical usage trends, and breakdowns by tool, device, model, session, or project. It lives wherever you look: the main window, the MacBook notch, the menu bar or system tray, the edge of the screen, a floating bubble, and native macOS widgets. ## Supported Tools Token usage, AI Tool Limits and session details from the AI coding tools and providers you already use:

## Why Token Monitor? Most usage monitors are useful on the machine they run on. Token Monitor is built for multi-device work: each device watches its own local logs, sends summary updates to your hub, and every connected widget sees token changes almost immediately. ## Quick Install On macOS, install through the official [Homebrew Cask](https://formulae.brew.sh/cask/token-monitor): ```bash brew install --cask token-monitor ``` Or download the app for macOS, Windows, or Linux from [GitHub Releases](https://github.com/Javis603/token-monitor/releases). Launch the app to start tracking this device locally, with no hub setup required. Notes, Custom balance endpoints, and data paths overridden by environment variables
- Paths above are the defaults. Token Monitor follows the same environment overrides Tokscale does — `$XDG_DATA_HOME` for the `~/.local/share/` roots, and per-tool variables such as `$CODEX_HOME`, `$GEMINI_CLI_HOME`, `$SENPI_CODING_AGENT_DIR`, `$SENPI_CODING_AGENT_SESSION_DIR`, `$GROK_HOME`, `$HERMES_HOME`, `$GOOSE_PATH_ROOT`, `$KIMI_CODE_HOME`, `$UNSLOTH_STUDIO_HOME`, `$LM_STUDIO_HOME`, `$DSH_HOME`, `$REASONIX_STATE_HOME`, `$REASONIX_HOME` and the `$CLINE_*` family. - Gemini CLI supports `$GEMINI_CLI_HOME` on the host; WSL discovery checks only the default Linux `~/.gemini/tmp/`. Fresh installs track it by default; existing saved tool selections must enable it in Settings → tools. - Muse Code subscription limits use `muse usage --json` from Muse Code 1.4.13+ and its existing sign-in. Missing allowance and API-key billing do not provide quota percentages. See the [Muse data-source notes](docs/providers/muse.md). - Goose counts all session usage on its creation day, including usage on later days. Remote goosed servers and custom scan paths are not supported. See [Goose source notes](docs/providers/goose.md). - CatPaw is off by default; enable it in Settings → tools. It reads domestic and overseas assistant databases on macOS and Windows. See [CatPaw source notes](docs/providers/catpaw.md) for paths and verification boundaries. - OmO Native tracks local session records from both OmO Native and standalone Senpi. A fresh install tracks it. An existing saved Tools selection does not gain it on upgrade; enable OmO Native in Settings → tools. Some child-task logs count toward usage but do not yet support Session Detail. See [OmO Native source notes](docs/providers/senpi.md). - LM Studio tracking currently covers OpenAI-compatible `/v1/chat/completions` and `/v1/responses` requests recorded in server logs. Conversations started from LM Studio's built-in Chat UI and native `/api/v1/chat` requests are not included. - Unsloth Studio tracks inference usage from `studio.db`: Studio chats and its local API. Local inference has zero API cost; recognized metered providers use Tokscale's price estimates. Training tokens are not included. See [Unsloth source notes](docs/providers/unsloth.md). - Devin tracks Devin CLI sessions from the local `sessions.db` and Devin Desktop agent sessions from `acp-events` ACP logs; where both cover the same session the CLI database is authoritative. Desktop coverage depends on the connected ACP agent: only agents that write `usage_update` events locally are counted, and Devin Desktop's default `devin-cloud` agent meters its usage server-side, so a default Desktop setup reports no Desktop tokens. Session titles and project attribution come from the CLI database. See [Devin source notes](docs/providers/devin.md). - Notion AI uses internal APIs with a manually pasted `token_v2` cookie and an explicit Business/Enterprise workspace ID. Only fixtures have been validated; a real response sample is unavailable and live authentication awaits approval. There is no automatic cookie retrieval or public API guarantee. See [Notion source notes](docs/providers/notion.md). - Manus reads a signed-in desktop session on macOS/Windows, or a manually supplied web session on any OS (including Linux). Monthly credits, refresh allowance and balance use the same undocumented internal endpoint, with no compatibility guarantee. See [Manus source notes](docs/providers/manus.md). - Hark reads the signed-in macOS desktop session, or a pasted session cookie on any OS. It shows account-level daily and monthly token pools. See [Hark source notes](docs/providers/hark.md). - MiniMax Code reads the local session history the CLI writes, under `~/.minimax` or `MINIMAX_DATA_DIR` / `MAVIS_DATA_DIR` (also `~/.mavis` and `~/.minimax-` / `~/.mavis-`), plus runs captured with `tokscale headless mcode`; a turn found in both counts once. - Command Code transcripts do not contain actual token counts or per-message model metadata. Token usage is estimated from transcript text, while model attribution and derived cost may reflect the currently configured model rather than the model historically used for each request. - The Cursor cache comes from Cursor's account-level usage export, so it covers usage from Cursor IDE, Cursor CLI, and Grok Bot. Token Monitor automatically detects accounts signed in through the Cursor desktop app and also supports adding accounts manually in Settings. The cache re-syncs automatically when stale, but newly finished sessions can take a few minutes to reach Cursor's dashboard, so recent usage may still appear with a delay. - Custom maps numeric JSON fields from one GET balance endpoint; OpenAI or Anthropic compatibility alone is not enough. - Qoder: the Qoder group in Settings → tools tracks the international and CN editions independently. Fresh installations track both; existing selections are preserved. The tool usage list combines them unless **Show versions separately** is on. International transcripts are read from `QODER_CONFIG_DIR/projects` (default `~/.qoder/projects`); CN transcripts from `TOKEN_MONITOR_QODER_CN_PROJECTS_PATH`, then `QODERCN_CONFIG_DIR/projects` (default `~/.qoder-cn/projects`). Only token counts recorded in transcripts are counted: managed-model rows that record credits without tokens are left out, and those credits stay in AI Tool Limits. Qoder CN CLI 1.1.62 has been reported to record future counters with `QODERCN_EXPOSE_TOKEN_USAGE=1`; existing records are not backfilled. Dynamic model slots such as `dfmodel` are shown as recorded. Older Qoder CN releases that stored usage only in SQLite are no longer collected; existing Token Monitor history files are kept. See [Qoder source notes](docs/providers/qodercn.md).
